Acknowledgements
The guidelines for the management of asthma in children and adolescents and of bronchiolitis in infants 
and young children were jointly prepared by the World Health Organization (WHO) Department of Sexual, 
Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing and the Department of Noncommunicable 
Diseases and Mental Health. Other departments represented on the WHO Steering Group include: the 
Department for HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis, Sexually Transmitted Infections; the Department of Nutrition 
and Food Safety; Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases; Science for Health; and the Department of 
Medicines and Health Products Policies and Standards.
WHO wishes to express its gratitude to the following Guideline Development Group members, the external 
reviewers, the guideline methodologist and the institutions that conducted the systematic reviews for their 
contributions to the development of the guidelines:
Guideline Development Group
WHO thanks the Guideline Development Group members who reviewed the evidence and made these 
recommendations: Mohamed Ahmed Abdullah, University of Khartoum, Khartoum, Sudan; Shams El 
Arifeen, International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Gillian 
Birchwood, The Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Bridgetown, Barbados; Trevor Duke, University of Melbourne, 
Faculty of Medicine, Dentistry and Health Sciences, Melbourne, Australia; Michael (Mike) English, University 
of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Grace Irimu, University of 
Nairobi, Nairobi, Kenya; Phillip Kasirye, Makerere University College of Health Sciences, Kampala, Uganda; 
Shanzida Khatun, National Institute of Advanced Nursing Education and Research, Dhaka, Bangladesh; 
Ajay Khera, EngenderHealth, New Delhi, India; Olga Komarova, National Medical Research Center of 
Children’s Health, Moscow, Russian Federation; Ida Safitri Laksono, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, 
Indonesia; Rakesh Lodha, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, India; Hesham Ben Masaud, 
General Practice Council, Libyan Board of Medical Specialties, Tripoli, Libya; Refiloe Masekela, University 
of KwaZulu Natal, Durban, South Africa; Hilda Mujuru, University of Zimbabwe, Harare, Zimbabwe; Mary 
Paiva, National Department of Health, Buka General Hospital, Buka, Autonomous Region of Bougainville, 
Papua New Guinea; Abdulkarim Rasa’a, Faculty of Medicine Sana’a University, Sana’a, Yemen; Sergey 
Sargsyan, Arabkir Medical Centre, Yerevan State Medical University, Yerevan, Armenia; Dheeraj Shah, 
University College of Medical Sciences and GTB Hospital, New Delhi, India; Gezahegn Nekatibeb Techane, 
Debre Berhan University, Debre Birhan, Ethiopia; and Dai Yaohua, Capital Institute of Paediatrics, Beijing, 
China. Many thanks to the co-chairs, Shams El Arifeen and Michael (Mike) English who chaired the Guideline 
Development Group meetings.
External Review Group
WHO wishes to acknowledge the following external reviewers: Allan Da Caen, Stollery Children’s Hospital 
University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada; Jayashree Muralidharan, Post Graduate Institute of 
Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, India; Obiageli Nnodu, University of Abuja, Abuja, Nigeria; 
Haroon Saloojee, Witwatersrand University, Johannesburg, South Africa; Anju Seth, Lady Hardinge Medical 
College and Associated Kalawati Saran Children’s Hospital, New Delhi, India; Varinder Singh, Lady Hardinge 
Medical College, New Delhi, India; and Ismail Ticklay, University of Zimbabwe, Harare, Zimbabwe.

Methodologists
WHO thanks the methodologists who guided the evidence reviewers and the Guideline Development Group 
discussions: Eddy Lang, University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada; Rebecca Morgan, McMaster University, 
Ontario, Canada; and Ife Babatunde, Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine, Cleveland, Ohio, 
United States of America.
Evidence synthesis team
WHO also wishes to acknowledge the following evidence synthesis and systematic review teams: Colin 
Powell, Ibtihal Abdelgadir, Khalid Mudawi, Ali Hamud, who are all affiliated to Sidra Medicine Doha, Doha, 
Qatar, for the asthma systematic reviews; and Ekwaro A. Obuku, Robert Apunyo, Victor Musiime, Rebecca 
Nantanda, Beatrice Odongkara, Alison Kinengyere, Julius Mubiru, Brenda Kawala, Kevin Ouma Ojiambo, 
Rachael Wangi, Ephraim Kisangala, Eve Namisango, Allen Eva Okullo, Regina Ndagire, Beatrice Basuuta and 
Lawrence Mbuagbwa, at the Africa Centre for Systematic Reviews and Knowledge Translation, Makerere 
University, Kampala, Uganda, for the bronchiolitis systematic reviews.
WHO Steering Group members
We acknowledge the following WHO staff who participated as members of the guidelines Steering Group 
in the development process: Prerna Banati (Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and 
Adolescent Health and Ageing), Jaden Bendabenda (Department of Nutrition and Food Safety), Bernadette 
Daelmans (Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing), Tarun 
Dua (Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health), Karen Edmond (Department of Sexual, 
Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing), Bianca Hemmingsen (Department of 
Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health), Ivy Kasirye (Department for HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis, 
Sexually Transmitted Infections), Peter Olumese (Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases), Martina 
Penazzato (Science for Health), Louise Puli (Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental 
Health), Nigel Rollins (Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and 
Ageing), Sarah Rylance (Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental Health), Sabine Verkuijl 
(Department for HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis, Sexually Transmitted Infections). Special thanks to WHO staff 
from regional and country offices: Jean-Marie Dangou, Teshome Desta and Roseline Doe, Regional Office 
for Africa; Pablo Duran, Regional Office for the Americas; Adela Mubasher and Khalid Siddeeg, Regional 
Office for the Eastern Mediterranean; Martin Will Weber, Regional Office for Europe; Deepti Agrawal and 
Neena Raina, Regional Office for South-East Asia and Daisuke Asai, Regional Office for the Western Pacific.
This work was coordinated by Sarah Rylance, Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental 
Health, WHO, and Wilson Were and Nuhu Yaqub, Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and 
Adolescent Health and Ageing, WHO. Special thanks for administrative support goes to Laure Cartillier, 
Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing, WHO. Leonore 
Greybe, Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch, South Africa and Lulu Muhe, independent consultant, 
Geneva, Switzerland, served as the rapporteurs and technical writers of this guideline.
Funding
The WHO guidelines for the management of asthma in children and adolescents, and bronchiolitis 
in  infants and young children, were funded by the Government of the Russian Federation through the 
maternal, newborn and paediatric quality of care improvement grant.

Glossary
Apnoea: Temporary cessation of breathing, especially during sleep.
Asthma: A heterogeneous disease, usually characterized by chronic airway inflammation and episodes of 
airway narrowing and obstruction causing breathing difficulties.
Bilevel positive airway pressure: A type of non-invasive ventilation that provides two levels of pressure: 
higher during inhalation and lower during exhalation.
Bronchiolitis: An acute viral infection of the lower respiratory tract that typically affects infants and 
children aged less than 2 years.
Continuous positive airway pressure: A treatment method that uses mild air pressure to keep the 
airways open.
Cyanosis: A bluish discolouration of the skin due to low oxygen levels in the blood.
Humidified high-flow nasal cannula: A method for delivery of up to 100% humidified and heated oxygen 
at high flow rates of up to 60 litres per minute.
Hypertonic saline: A highly concentrated saline water solution used in nebulization to help relieve 
wheezing and breathing difficulty.
Hypoxaemia: Low levels of oxygen in the blood.
Moderate paediatric asthma exacerbation : A sudden increase in asthma symptoms, associated with: 
peak expiratory flow >50% best or predicted, increased respiratory rate (<30/min), increased heart rate 
(100–120/min), able to complete sentences in one breath and oxygen saturation (on air) 90–95%. These 
parameters are applicable to children aged ≥6 years.1
Nebulization: A method of administering medication in the form of a mist inhaled into the lungs.
Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation: A method of oxygen delivery of positive pressure ventilation 
via a tight-fitting mask that covers the nose or both the nose and mouth without the need for endotracheal 
intubation.
Non-invasive ventilation: A method of providing ventilatory support without the need for endotracheal 
intubation.
Peripheral capillary oxygen saturation: A measure of the oxygen saturation level in the blood.
Prodrome: An early symptom indicating the onset of a disease.
Respiratory distress: Difficulty in breathing, often characterized by rapid breathing and use of accessory 
muscles.
Respiratory syncytial virus: A common virus that causes bronchiolitis and other respiratory infections in 
young children.
1  For further details, see Table 2.

Severe paediatric asthma exacerbation: A sudden increase in asthma symptoms, associated with: peak 
expiratory flow ≤50% best or predicted, increased respiratory rate (>30/min), increased heart rate (>120/
min), use of accessory breathing muscles, inability to complete sentences in one breath, decreased oxygen 
saturation (on air) <90%. These parameters are applicable to children aged ≥6 years.1
Spacer: A device used with an inhaler to help deliver medication to the lungs more effectively.
Standard first-line therapy: The initial treatment of acute asthma with inhaled bronchodilators and 
systemic corticosteroids.
Tachycardia: Abnormally rapid heart rate.
Tachypnoea: Abnormally rapid breathing.
Ventilator-induced lung injury: Lung damage that occurs as a result of mechanical ventilation.
Wheezing: A high-pitched whistling sound made while breathing, often associated with respiratory 
conditions.

pages.raw_text:
Summary of recommendations
Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Additional treatment to standard first-line therapy for 
paediatric asthma exacerbations
Recommendation 1a:  Nebulized ipratropium bromide should be added to standard first-line therapy 
with inhaled short-acting beta2 agonists (SABA) and systemic corticosteroids for severe paediatric asthma 
exacerbations in health facilities.
Recommendation 1b: Nebulized ipratropium bromide should be added for moderate paediatric asthma 
exacerbations not responsive to initial standard first-line therapy with inhaled SABA and systemic 
corticosteroids in health facilities.
Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• Ipratropium bromide should be given in addition to standard inhaled or nebulized SABA and systemic 
corticosteroids in cases where children are not responding or when the severity of the exacerbation is 
extreme and impending collapse is likely.
• It is essential that first-level health care providers are trained and competent to assess the severity of 
an acute asthma exacerbation, start first-line therapy appropriately and monitor response.
• The results of the systematic review favoured the use of nebulized ipratropium bromide but could not 
confirm similar effects with administration via metered-dose inhaler (MDI), mask and spacer.
Second-line therapy options for paediatric asthma 
exacerbations
Recommendation 2: Intravenous (IV) magnesium sulfate (as a single short infusion) should be used as 
second-line therapy for severe paediatric asthma exacerbations, and for moderate exacerbations not 
responsive to standard first-line therapy with inhaled/nebulized medicines (SABA and ipratropium) and 
systemic corticosteroids in health care facilities.
Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence.

pages.raw_text:
Remarks
• Current evidence does not support the use of inhaled magnesium sulfate, and intramuscular (IM) 
magnesium sulfate has not been studied in acute asthma exacerbations.
• IV infusion of magnesium sulfate relaxes smooth muscle and may result in hypotension, a side-effect 
commonly seen with the use of IM magnesium sulfate in pregnant women.
• It is advised that magnesium sulfate should be diluted in a compatible solution and administered as a 
single IV infusion over 20 minutes.
• The most frequent dosing regime was 50 mg/kg of magnesium sulfate diluted in 100 mL normal saline 
with a maximum dose of 2 g administered over 20–30 minutes, although it has been suggested that 
higher doses up to 100 mg/kg and prolonged infusions may be beneficial life-threatening asthma.
• Regular blood pressure monitoring should be included in the routine observations of children receiving 
IV magnesium sulfate.
Recommendation 3: IV aminophylline should not be used as second-line therapy for severe paediatric 
asthma exacerbations in health facilities if alternative second-line options are available.
Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• The restricted use of aminophylline should be accompanied by the availability of appropriate inhaled 
SABA and systemic corticosteroids for the management of acute asthma exacerbation across all 
settings.
• In resource-restricted and rural settings aminophylline may be the only available agent for the 
management of acute asthma exacerbations.
• If the decision is made to use aminophylline, due to lack of alternatives, adequate monitoring and anti-
emetics should be used to mitigate the risk of side-effects.
No recommendation: WHO makes no recommendation on the use of subcutaneous adrenaline in the 
management of acute asthma.
Remarks
• Adrenaline should be reserved for patients who present with symptoms and signs consistent with 
severe allergic reactions.
• The use of IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis is described in WHO’s Pocket book of hospital care for children 
(1) and the Integrated management of adolescent and adult illness (2).
Recommendation 4: IV SABA should be used as a potential second-line therapy for severe paediatric 
asthma exacerbations in addition to standard first-line therapy with inhaled/nebulized medicines (SABA 
and ipratropium) and systemic corticosteroids in health care facilities.
Strong recommendation, high-certainty evidence.

pages.raw_text:
Recommendation 6: Combination inhaler (steroid plus fast-onset long-acting beta2 agonist (LABA)) 
MART should be considered for children with persistent asthma symptoms requiring regular inhaled 
corticosteroid (ICS) treatment.
Conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• Although evidence was considered for children aged 4–11 years, current formulations are licensed for 
children aged ≥6 years; hence, the recommendation is restricted to children aged 6–11 years.
Combination maintenance and reliever therapy 
(MART) for the long-term management of asthma
Remarks
• IV SABA can be used as a potential second-line therapy, depending on the availability of other options. 
IV magnesium sulfate would be preferred as second-line therapy, if available (see Recommendation 
5).
• IV SABA is most likely to be used in the PICU or settings where the infrastructure and monitoring 
already exist.
• Careful clinical monitoring is recommended to ensure the early identification and management of 
possible cardiovascular adverse effects, such as tachycardia, hypotension and arrhythmias.
• Where resources are available, it is advisable to have continuous electrocardiogram monitoring, and 
check serum electrolytes (hypokalaemia) and lactate.
Preferred second- and third-line therapy for paediatric 
asthma exacerbations
Recommendation 5: IV magnesium sulfate should be the preferred option for second-line therapy and IV 
SABA the preferred option for third-line therapy in severe paediatric asthma exacerbations not responding 
to standard first-line therapy.
Conditional recommendation, very low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• A pragmatic stepwise approach to second-line therapies would be appropriate, and allow practitioners 
to choose the best possible option for their setting.
• In settings where neither preferred option is available, IV aminophylline may be considered as 
additional therapy in severe asthma exacerbations not responding to standard first-line therapy.

pages.raw_text:
• Current evidence supports the use of combination inhaler (steroid plus fast-onset LABA) MART for 
children with persistent asthma symptoms who are already taking or planning to start regular ICS 
therapy.
• The use of a combination inhaler results in a potentially simpler regime, which may be more easily 
followed by both patients and prescribers.
• Children with infrequent symptoms should use SABA as needed, considering the concomitant 
intermittent use of ICS.
Recommendations for the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young 
children 
Guiding principle for using clinical symptoms and signs in 
supporting a probable diagnosis of bronchiolitis in an infant or 
child
Good practice statement 1: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting with cough and 
difficulty in breathing, a comprehensive history and assessment of clinical signs and symptoms should 
be done. A diagnosis of bronchiolitis can be suspected if they have a history of a prodrome of an upper 
respiratory tract infection with rhinitis or coryza and cough, followed by respiratory distress with a low-
grade fever, and any presence of tachypnoea (fast breathing), chest indrawing and diffuse wheeze or 
crackles on auscultation.
Remarks
• Assessment of clinical signs should include the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) (3) 
general danger signs,2 cyanosis, respiratory rate, looking for chest indrawing, listening for a wheeze 
or crackles, and measuring oxygen saturation.
• Infants with viral bronchiolitis are usually not very ill looking, and many have a prolonged expiratory 
phase of breathing associated with wheeze.
• During a respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) outbreak, a higher index of suspicion should be maintained 
in the differential diagnosis for infants presenting with respiratory symptoms.
• A comprehensive history should also elicit presence of any risk factors and comorbidities, such as 
prematurity, children who are immunocompromized, and children with asthma or reactive airway 
disease, chronic lung disease, chronic neurological conditions or congenital heart conditions, and 
breastfeeding status.
2  The IMCI general danger signs are: inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, experiencing convulsions and being lethargic 
or unconscious.

pages.raw_text:
Guiding principle for assessing infants and children with 
suspected bronchiolitis for hospital admission
 
Good practice statement 2: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting with suspected 
bronchiolitis, clinicians should perform a comprehensive assessment for presence of risk factors and signs 
of severe disease.
Indications for admissions include: Signs of severe disease, which include IMCI general danger signs, 3 
high temperature of ≥38°C, central cyanosis or peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2) <90%, severe 
respiratory distress, apnoea or history of apnoea, and presence of risk factors for severe disease which 
include comorbidities,a prematurity and age <3 months.
Remarks
• The indications for admission found in the review are mostly similar to the current WHO guideline 
recommendations for the admission of severe pneumonia (1).
• Clinicians should avoid unwarranted admissions that may lead to exposure to nosocomial infections 
and avoidable hospital care costs.
• Local context should be taken into consideration, particularly the availability of follow-up or its 
accessibility, including travelling distances for patients, for example.
• The temperature threshold of ≥38°C in cases of suspected bronchiolitis is significant and might be 
justification for admission or close observation.
• Comorbidities to consider in the history include: congenital cardiac lesions, chronic lung disease, 
cerebral palsy and neurological conditions.
Use of chest X-ray in the clinical management of bronchiolitis
Recommendation 1: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting or hospitalized with 
suspected bronchiolitis, routine use of chest X-ray is not suggested for the initial diagnosis and 
management of bronchiolitis.
Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence.
3  The IMCI general danger signs are: inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, experiencing convulsions and being lethargic 
or unconscious.
xiv

pages.raw_text:
Remarks
• Chest X-ray for hospitalized infants and children with suspected bronchiolitis should only be considered 
on a case-by-case basis; for example, in the following clinical situations:
• if there is high suspicion for other alternate diagnosis or underlying cardiac or chronic lung 
disease related to risk factors elicited on history or physical examination;
• if a child fails to respond to treatment or persistent symptoms for more than 2 weeks without 
improvement;
• if there is suspected bacterial superinfection or recurrent episodes of pneumonia;
• if there is severe respiratory distress or severe hypoxaemia requiring admission to high care or 
intensive care;
• where a complication, such as effusion or pneumothorax, may be suspected; for example, when 
there are unilateral signs of severe dullness to percussion or absent breath sounds.
Administration of supplemental oxygen through nasal bubble 
continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
No recommendation: WHO makes no recommendation on the use of nasal bubble CPAP to administer 
oxygen rather than standard flow oxygen (SFO) through nasal prongs/face mask/headbox for better 
clinical outcomes.
Humidified high-flow oxygen versus SFO
Recommendation 2: In infants and children aged less than 2 years, hospitalized with acute bronchiolitis 
with hypoxaemia, humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HHFNC) oxygen is suggested rather than SFO.
Condition recommendation, low certainty of evidence.
Remarks
• In most cases, children with acute bronchiolitis should be started on standard low-flow oxygen, which 
is very often effective in resolving the hypoxaemia.
• HHFNC oxygen is indicated where, despite standard low-flow oxygen therapy, the infant has persisting 
hypoxaemia (SpO2 <90%) or severe respiratory distress.

pages.raw_text:
Nebulized hypertonic (3%) saline versus no hypertonic saline
Recommendation 3: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting or hospitalized with 
bronchiolitis, a trial of nebulized hypertonic saline (3%) is suggested rather than no nebulization.
Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence.
Remarks
• The majority of studies used a comparison with normal saline which may underestimate the effect of 
hypertonic saline.
• A trial of nebulized hypertonic saline in an individual patient may aid in clearance of secretions, but 
might not always be effective.
• Health facilities experience overcrowding during peak RSV season, making any reduction in the length 
of hospital stays through the use of nebulized hypertonic saline especially valuable.
• Health care workers should be aware that hypertonic saline can induce bronchoconstriction and may 
often require co-administration with bronchodilators.
xvi

pages.raw_text: 1. Introduction
pages.cleaned_text: 1. Introduction

pages.raw_text:
Respiratory illness is a leading cause of morbidity among children globally, with both acute and chronic 
conditions contributing substantially to outpatient visits and hospital admissions throughout infancy, 
childhood and adolescence (4). Among the diverse clinical presentations of paediatric respiratory disease, 
wheeze is one of the most frequent and clinically important. Wheeze, defined as a high-pitched, musical 
sound produced by airflow through narrowed lower airways during expiration, is a common manifestation 
of multiple paediatric respiratory disorders.
In children aged less than 2 years, wheeze most commonly occurs in the context of acute viral bronchiolitis 
or other causes of small-airway obstruction. In older children and adolescents, wheeze is more often 
associated with asthma and other chronic airway diseases. Although these conditions differ in their 
underlying pathophysiology and natural history, they often present with similar clinical features, including 
wheeze, tachypnoea, chest indrawing and varying degrees of hypoxaemia, particularly during acute 
episodes.
Bronchiolitis typically affects infants in the first 2 years of life, with the highest incidence occurring in the 
first year (5). It is characterized by acute inflammation of the small airways, most often triggered by viral 
infection, leading to airway obstruction, increased work of breathing and impaired gas exchange. Asthma, 
in contrast, is a chronic inflammatory airway disease that manifests through recurrent episodes of wheeze, 
cough, chest tightness and breathlessness, with symptoms that vary in severity and over time.
Because bronchiolitis and asthma share overlapping clinical features especially wheeze and respiratory 
distress, distinguishing between them in routine clinical practice can be challenging, particularly in younger 
children and in settings with limited diagnostic capacity. These overlaps are most evident during acute 
presentations, when rapid decisions about treatment and referral must be made.

childhood: asthma and bronchiolitis; and provides evidence-based recommendations to support accurate 
assessment, appropriate treatment and effective management across the age spectrum from infancy to 
adolescence.
1.1 Purpose and rationale
1.1.1 Asthma
Asthma control is frequently suboptimal, particularly in low-resource settings (6). Uncontrolled asthma 
symptoms lead to school absence and negatively affect children’s educational and social opportunities (6), 
while emergency health care use and hospitalization impose substantial costs on families, health systems 
and the wider economy. In addition to the burden measured in disability-adjusted life years, asthma 
contributes significantly to avoidable morbidity and premature mortality (8). To make progress towards 
Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target 3.4, which calls for a one third reduction in premature mortality 
from noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), it is essential to strengthen both acute and long-term asthma 
care, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where most asthma-related deaths occur (9). The 
importance of effective acute and chronic asthma treatment as priority interventions to reduce premature 
mortality has been underscored by initiatives such as NCD Countdown 2030 (10).
Current WHO guidance on asthma management is provided in the Pocket book of hospital care for 
children (1), which focuses primarily on acute care, and in the WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable 
Disease (PEN) interventions for primary health care (11). However, there is a need to ensure that these 
recommendations reflect the current evidence base and are aligned with the WHO Model List of Essential 
Medicines for Children (EMLc), particularly in relation to medicines and treatment strategies for children 
and adolescents (12).

1.1.2 Bronchiolitis
Bronchiolitis is a common paediatric illness affecting children aged less than 2 years and is one of the 
leading causes of hospital admission in infancy. It is responsible for substantial increases in health care 
utilization, including oxygen use, respiratory support and inpatient care, resulting in significant medical 
costs and pressure on health systems. In LMICs, bronchiolitis contributes to child mortality through 
hypoxaemia, respiratory failure and complications of severe illness. To achieve SDG target 3.2, which aims 
to end preventable deaths of neonates and children aged less than 5 years, it is essential to improve the 
quality and consistency of bronchiolitis care, particularly in settings with limited resources.
At present, there are no stand-alone WHO guidelines dedicated specifically to the management of 
bronchiolitis, although the condition is addressed within the Pocket book of hospital care for children (1). 
There is also rapidly evolving evidence regarding key aspects of bronchiolitis management, including 
the role of nebulized hypertonic saline, high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy and continuous 
positive airway pressure (CPAP) in the escalation of care and prevention of respiratory failure (13). This 
evolving evidence base has not yet been clearly or consistently translated into global guidance. There is 
therefore a need to ensure that recommendations for bronchiolitis reflect current best evidence and are 
aligned with the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children (12) and the Interagency list of medical 
devices for essential interventions for reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (14).
Asthma and bronchiolitis account for a large proportion of paediatric respiratory morbidity, health care 
utilization and preventable mortality. Both conditions are prevalent and place substantial demands on 
health systems, and require timely, evidence-based management to improve outcomes. A WHO guideline 
that provides up-to-date, aligned, and context-appropriate recommendations for the management of 
asthma and bronchiolitis is therefore essential to support countries in achieving their child health and 
NCD targets under the SDGs.

2. Process and 
methods

pages.raw_text:
The guidelines for the management of asthma in children and adolescents, and bronchiolitis in infants 
and young children were developed in accordance with the principles and procedures outlined in the WHO 
handbook for guideline development (15). The guideline development process followed WHO’s standard 
steps, which include: (i) defining the general scope of the recommendations; (ii) identifying contributors and 
establishing the Guideline Development Group (GDG); (iii) formulating key questions and outcomes using 
the population, intervention, comparison and outcome (PICO) format; (iv) conducting systematic evidence 
reviews; (v) assessing the certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, 
Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach; (vi) formulating recommendations and drafting of the 
guideline narrative; (vii) reviewing and approving the recommendations through the GDG; (viii) conducting 
external peer review; (ix) submitting the guideline for review and approval by WHO’s Guidelines Review 
Committee; and (x) finalizing and disseminating the final recommendations.
2.1 Contributors
A diverse group of contributors participated in the guideline development process, including clinical 
experts, methodologists, health system specialists and representatives from WHO headquarters and 
its regional and country offices. All contributors were selected based on their expertise and experience, 
and their roles were clearly defined in line with WHO policies to ensure effectiveness, transparency and 
minimize bias (Annex 1).
The WHO Steering Group comprised members from relevant technical units at WHO headquarters and 
WHO’s regional and country offices. The WHO Steering Group provided technical oversight, coordinated 
the process and supported project management. This Group also established the general scope of the 
guideline, drafted potential key questions and identified and selected the GDG members.
The GDG included members from all WHO regions and a range of professional backgrounds. Their expertise 
covered the clinical management of asthma and bronchiolitis, as well as health systems, programme 
implementation and patient care. The GDG was supported by a guideline methodologist, who ensured 
methodological rigour throughout the process.
Systematic review teams were commissioned to synthesize the evidence for each key question. An External 
Review Group, composed of technical and implementation experts, reviewed the final draft of the guideline 
and provided feedback on content and presentation.
2.2 Management of conflict of interest
In accordance with the WHO handbook for guideline development (15), all individuals involved in the guideline 
development process, including members of the GDG, external reviewers and contributors, were required 
to disclose any potential conflicts of interest. These disclosures were reviewed by WHO staff and assessed 
for relevance and severity. Where a conflict of interest was identified, appropriate measures were taken 
to manage it, including exclusion from specific discussions or decisions, or full recusal from participation. 
The objective was to ensure transparency, maintain the integrity of the guideline development process and 
safeguard against undue influence. All conflict-of-interest declarations and management decisions were 
documented and are available upon request. Only individuals with no significant conflicts of interest were 
formally invited to join the GDG or External Review Group. Further details are provided in Annex 1.

2.3 Evidence retrieval and synthesis
At the initial two virtual GDG meetings, the GDG established the scope of the guideline; the key questions, 
using the PICO format; and identified key outcomes. Systematic reviews were commissioned to address 
each of the prioritized PICO questions (see annexes 2 and 3). These reviews adhered to Cochrane methods 
and standards and were conducted by independent review teams (16). The GRADE approach was used 
to assess the certainty of evidence for each critical and important outcome (17). Detailed methods are 
described in the respective systematic reviews (Web Annex (18)).
2.4 Formulation of recommendations
The GDG meet virtually and in person between July 2023 and February 2024 to review the evidence and 
formulate recommendations. The meetings were chaired by a GDG member and facilitated by the guideline 
methodologist. The GDG used an explicit evidence-to-decision framework to guide discussions and ensure 
transparency in decision-making.
Recommendations were based on a balance of benefits and harms, the certainty of evidence, values and 
preferences, acceptability, feasibility, resource use and equity considerations. Each recommendation was 
classified as either strong or conditional, with:
• a strong recommendation indicating high confidence that the desirable effects outweigh the 
undesirable effects; and
• a conditional recommendation reflecting less certainty, acknowledging that the balance of desirable 
effects may vary on context or stakeholder values. The choices of individuals and policy or decision-
makers will vary according to the relative values placed on the outcomes, acceptability, resources and 
other considerations.
• Consensus was the primary method for decision-making. All GDG members present had to agree on 
the final wording and the strength of each recommendation. If consensus could not be reached, a 
vote was planned as the fallback approach. Only GDG members participated in the decision-making 
process, although WHO staff, the methodologist and observers contributed to discussions.
• The GDG also identified research gaps during the formulation process. These reflect the uncertainties 
in the evidence base and highlight areas where further research could improve future guideline 
development and clinical decision-making. These research gaps are not prioritized or exhaustive but 
are intended to inform future research agendas.
• Following the GDG meeting, the guideline writer drafted the narrative sections, which were reviewed 
and approved by the GDG, and then submitted for external peer review by the External Review Group. 
After incorporating the feedback, the final recommendations were reviewed and approved by WHO’s 
Guidelines Review Committee and prepared for publication and dissemination.

3. Management of 
asthma in children

pages.raw_text:
Asthma is a chronic respiratory illness, and one of the main NCDs included in WHO’s Global Action Plan for the 
Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases 2013–2030 (19). Every year, an estimated 426 000 people 
die from asthma, with half of these deaths in people aged less than 70 years. Over 95% of these premature 
deaths occur in LMICs (4). Asthma is a major cause of morbidity in young people and ranks among the 
leading causes of disability-adjusted life years worldwide (20). According to the Global Asthma Network 
Phase I study, about one in 20 school-aged children have severe asthma symptoms, with prevalence 
varying between and within countries (21).
The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) defines asthma as “a heterogeneous disease, usually characterized 
by chronic airway inflammation. It is defined by the history of respiratory symptoms, such as wheeze, 
shortness of breath, chest tightness and cough, that vary over time and in intensity, together with variable 
airflow limitation” (22).
Symptoms of asthma are typically worse at night and in the early morning, and are due to airway smooth 
muscle constriction, also known as bronchoconstriction, and inflammation of the airway lining. These 
symptoms are usually mild and may be controlled with medicine and avoidance of known allergens, but 
they can result in potentially life-threatening exacerbations.
Children and adolescents with asthma may experience short-term worsening of their asthma symptoms, 
with a progressive increase in wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness and cough. These episodes 
are known as acute asthma, attacks, flare-ups or exacerbations. In this document, the term exacerbation 
will be used. Acute asthma is commonly triggered by viral respiratory tract infections, exercise, change in 
weather and exposure to allergens (such as tree and grass pollen) and irritants (such as tobacco smoke or 
air pollution) (22).
Treatment aims to reduce airway smooth muscle constriction using bronchodilators and to reduce 
airway inflammation using corticosteroids. Inhaled bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are 
recommended for the long-term asthma management in the WHO package of essential noncommunicable 
(PEN) disease interventions for primary health care (11). During an acute episode, people with asthma need 
to change their usual treatment; for example, increasing their use of inhaled short-acting bronchodilators 
and taking a short course of systemic corticosteroids. More severe cases may require emergency 
treatment in a health facility and admission to hospital. However, effective asthma management involves 
a holistic approach that addresses both pharmacological and non-pharmacological management, as well 
as education and self-management aspects. Working in partnership with children and families is key in 
promoting good outcomes. Educating people with asthma on how to take the treatment effectively, how 
to avoid triggers, what their modifiable risk factors are, and the actions to take during acute exacerbations 
via personalized asthma action plans is essential.
3.1 Acute management of asthma
Inhaled bronchodilators are the first step in treating an acute asthma exacerbation. Short-acting beta 2 
agonists (SABA) should be started as initial therapy at the onset of acute symptoms (cough, wheeze, 
difficulty breathing). Children with asthma should have access to a SABA inhaler and a plan of how to use 
it when an exacerbation occurs. A mild exacerbation can usually be managed at home if symptoms are 
relieved promptly with inhaled SABA.
If symptoms do not subside rapidly, patients are advised to seek medical review to assess the severity of 
the exacerbation. Assessment and classification of severity as mild, moderate, severe and life-threatening 
asthma depend on clinical signs including heart rate, respiratory rate, work of breathing, ability to talk, 
mental state and measuring oxygen saturation and peak expiratory flow (PEF) (if possible). The global and 
national guidelines available differ slightly in their classification of asthma exacerbation severity, although 
the overall clinical pictures described are broadly consistent (Table 1) (22-25).

the overall clinical pictures described are broadly consistent (Table 1) (22-25).

For patients with moderate or severe symptoms, prompt treatment with oral corticosteroids, for example, 
prednisolone or dexamethasone is advised. Administration of corticosteroids significantly reduces the 
need for hospital admission when given within 1 hour of presentation for emergency care and reduces 
relapse of symptoms (26, 27). In patients who are not able to tolerate oral medication, the intravenous (IV) 
or intramuscular (IM) route can be considered.
The initial treatment of acute asthma with inhaled bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids is referred 
to in this document as standard first-line therapy.
3.2 Long-term management of asthma
The long-term management of asthma with inhaled bronchodilators and ICS has been standard practice 
for decades. However, evidence from large multi-centred RCTs, including mostly adults and older children, 
suggest that there should be changes in the way that these medicines are used (22); hence, the need to 
review the available evidence for children and adolescents.
3.3 Scope and target audience
This guideline reviews the current evidence to inform the recommendations for children and adolescents 
aged <19 years diagnosed with asthma. It is not intended to encompass all aspects of the acute 
management and the long-term management of asthma, but builds on existing recommendations. The 
recommendations on acute management relate to the emergency treatment of an asthma exacerbation 
in a health care facility, while the recommendations for long-term management relate to the ongoing 
treatment of the chronic condition with inhaled medicines, aiming at controlling symptoms and avoiding 
acute exacerbations. Therefore, for this guideline, the recommendations encompass the following topic 
areas:
• additional treatment to standard first-line therapy for paediatric asthma exacerbations;
• potential second-line therapy options for paediatric asthma exacerbations;
• preferred second- and third-line therapy for paediatric asthma exacerbations; and
• combination maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) for the long-term management of asthma.
The recommendations cover the options for inhaled and IV treatment in addition to standard first-line 
therapy with inhaled bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids. They also take into consideration the 
need for early intervention with effective treatment to avoid potentially fatal outcomes, particularly in 
resource-limited settings where it may not be possible to escalate the level of care provided. The prioritized 
PICO questions discussed in section 4 are outlined in Annex 1.

4.1 Additional treatment to standard first-line therapy for paediatric 
asthma exacerbations
4.1.2 Inhaled or nebulized ipratropium bromide
Background
The inhaled anti-cholinergic, ipratropium bromide, is a quaternary ammonium derivative of atropine 
which reduces mucosal oedema and secretions and relieves cholinergic bronchomotor tone, resulting in 
bronchodilation. It is commonly used for the relief of bronchoconstriction due to limited absorption from the 
airways and minimal systemic effects (28). The antagonistic effect of ipratropium bromide on acetylcholine 
receptors in the airways has also been proposed to be particularly beneficial in viral infections, which cause 
acute asthma exacerbations by modifying these receptors (29). Inhaled ipratropium bromide is typically 
administered with an oxygen-driven nebulizer, but a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with a mask and spacer is 
a commonly used alternative in low-resource settings where an oxygen supply is unavailable (30).
Ipratropium bromide is seldom used on its own and a review of six clinical trials in 171 children suggested 
that it is inferior to inhaled SABA for the management of acute asthma exacerbations in children aged 
older than 2 years (31). A combination of inhaled SABA and ipratropium bromide performed better than 
ipratropium bromide alone (treatment failure, odds ratio (OR): 2.65; 95% confidence interval (CI): −1.2 to 
5.88) in this population (31). When nebulized ipratropium bromide was added to SABA in a review of 472 
children aged 1–18 years hospitalized with acute asthma, no evidence of benefit for length of hospital stay 
(mean difference (MD): −0.28 hours; 95% CI: −5.07 to 4.52) or response to therapy was found (32). However, 
in a systematic review assessing combination inhalation of ipratropium bromide and SABA for the initial 
treatment of acute asthma in 2497 children, the addition of ipratropium bromide to SABA reduced the risk 
of hospital admission significantly (relative risk (RR): 0.73; 95% CI: 0.63–0.85) and a trend towards greater 
effect with increased severity was observed but did not reach statistical significance (33). No severe adverse 
effects were attributed to ipratropium bromide in any of the systematic reviews, confirming its favourable 
safety profile.
The evidence supporting ipratropium bromide as an effective and safe bronchodilator, and its use in 
combination with SABA inhalations, requires further investigation to define its use as an additional 
treatment in children who present with acute asthma exacerbations.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Recommendation 1a: 
Nebulized ipratropium bromide should be added to standard first-line therapy with inhaled 
SABA and systemic corticosteroids for severe paediatric asthma exacerbations in health 
facilities.
Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence.
Recommendation 1b: 
Nebulized ipratropium bromide should be added for moderate paediatric asthma 
exacerbations not responsive to initial standard first-line therapy with inhaled SABA and 
systemic corticosteroids in health facilities.
Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• Ipratropium bromide should be given in addition to standard inhaled or nebulized SABA 
and systemic corticosteroids in cases where children are not responding or when the 
severity of the exacerbation is extreme and impending collapse is likely.
• It is essential that first-level health care providers are trained and competent to assess 
the severity of an acute asthma exacerbation, start first-line therapy appropriately and 
monitor response.
• The results of the systematic review favoured the use of nebulized ipratropium bromide 
but could not confirm similar effects with administration via MDI, mask and spacer.
Justification
The review found, with moderate-certainty evidence, that less hospitalization (relative risk reduction (RRR): 
5.2%) is needed when nebulized ipratropium bromide is used in addition to standard first-line therapy. 
However, when inhaled ipratropium bromide was compared to placebo, the hospitalization rate was similar 
(very low-certainty evidence), but a cost benefit is likely (34-36). The GDG considered that length of hospital 
stay may be influenced by various aspects of health care delivery (timing of ward rounds, availability of a 
pharmacist) and is not solely dependent on the underlying disease process. There was significant variability 
in the methods used to quantify improvements in symptoms, and low to very low evidence that it may 
favour ipratropium bromide. Additional literature considered suggests that most providers and caregivers 
value a reduction in hospitalization and probable improvement in asthma symptoms over a small risk of 
non-severe adverse effects and that the use of ipratropium bromide is cost-effective when used for severe 
exacerbations (37).

Due to the potentially life-threatening nature of acute asthma exacerbations, early intervention is imperative 
to treatment success. Therefore, given the moderate desirable effects, the small increase in non-severe 
adverse events, and values, acceptability, equity and feasibility which all favour the use of ipratropium 
bromide, the GDG made a strong recommendation in favour of the use of ipratropium bromide.
Summary of evidence
The evidence reviewed included 24 studies of 3238 children aged 18 years and younger with acute asthma 
exacerbation, as defined by the study criteria. Four studies were conducted in lower-middle-income 
countries (India, Pakistan) (38-41) and three in upper-middle-income countries (Mexico, Thailand, Türkiye) 
(42-44). Children were recruited from emergency and outpatient departments and all children received and 
failed to improve on standard first-line therapy, including at least three inhalations of SABA and systemic 
corticosteroids. The addition of ipratropium bromide to standard first-line therapy was compared to 
standard first-line therapy alone or in addition to placebo. Ipratropium bromide was typically administered 
as a nebulization within the first hour after presentation, but the dosing varied considerably. The critical 
outcomes under investigation included hospitalization, escalation of care (mechanical ventilation or 
paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission), length of hospital stay, morbidity (symptom improvement) 
and adverse effects.
Compared to placebo, the group receiving nebulized ipratropium bromide had a reduced need for 
hospitalization (RR: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.64–0.9, moderate-certainty evidence) (38, 42, 43, 45-49),  but there was 
no difference in PICU admissions (RR: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.35–2.32, low-certainty evidence) (48, 50) or length of 
hospital stay in hours (MD: 1.75; 95% CI: −0.87 to 4.36, high-certainty evidence) (51-54)  between groups. 
One study included children with moderate asthma exacerbation and compared inhaled ipratropium 
bromide administered with an MDI to placebo (RR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.94–1.27) and did not show a benefit 
in hospitalization (very low-quality evidence) (55). Improvements in symptoms were measured using 
PEF measurement differences after interventions in seven trials (MD: 8.56; 95% CI: 1.24–15.88, very low-
certainty evidence) (40-42, 47, 53, 56, 57); forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1) % predicted in three 
trials (MD: 15.64; 95% CI: −7.49 to 38.77, very low-certainty evidence) (40, 56, 58); and clinical asthma score 
improvement (MD: −0.38; 95% CI: −0.63 to −0.12, low-certainty evidence) in eight trials (39, 40, 42, 47, 
51, 53, 56, 57). Adverse events included nausea, vomiting, headaches, dry mouth, abdominal pain and 
conjunctivitis and occurred in both groups (RR: 1.39; 95% CI: 0.95–2.05, moderate-certainty evidence) (38, 
43, 45, 46, 49, 52, 55, 58).
Benefits and desirable effects
The addition of nebulized ipratropium bromide to standard acute asthma therapy reduced the hospitalization 
(RRR: 5.2%) of children presenting with asthma exacerbation. However, the addition of ipratropium bromide 
did not reduce the need for PICU admission (RR: 0.91) or length of hospital stay. The GDG considered that 
the length of hospital stay may be influenced by various aspects of health care delivery (timing of ward 
rounds, availability of a pharmacist) and is not solely dependent on the underlying disease process. An 
improvement in symptoms was evaluated by several proxy measures including a significant improvement 
seen in PEF (MD: 8.56) and reduction of clinical asthma severity scores (MD: −0.38), but there was no 
meaningful difference in FEV 1 % predicted (MD: 15.64) between the groups. These measurements were 
considered too heterogeneous to influence the recommendation. The GDG also noted that the greater 
effect of ipratropium bromide and SABA synergism with increased asthma exacerbation severity previously 
observed was not evaluated by the systematic review but may be relevant.
The GDG judged the desirable effects of ipratropium bromide in addition to standard first-line therapy in 
acute asthma exacerbations as moderate (low-certainty evidence).

Harms and undesirable effects
Minor adverse effects were observed equally in both the ipratropium bromide and placebo groups (RR: 
1.39) and the GDG therefore judged the undesirable effects associated with ipratropium bromide to be 
small (moderate-certainty evidence).
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG agreed that most providers and caregivers would 
value a reduction in hospitalization and probable improvement in asthma symptoms over a small risk of 
minor adverse effects. This view is supported by a qualitative study of parents and caregivers of children 
presenting to hospital with a severe acute exacerbation of asthma in 12 countries (high- and middle-
income) (37). Caregivers highlighted length of hospital stay, intensive care unit (ICU) or high dependence 
unit admission, and treatment costs as the most important outcomes. The GDG considered that a reduction 
in hospitalization would equate to a reduced hospital stay.
Resources required:  Several studies have previously evaluated the cost and cost-effectiveness of 
ipratropium bromide in addition to standard acute asthma management in LMICs (34-36) . These studies 
suggest that the provision of ipratropium bromide in addition to inhaled SABA delivered using a mask 
and spacer device is more beneficial financially that providing the same drugs in nebulized form (35, 
36). Additionally, the cost benefit is attributed to a reduction in hospitalization and is observed when 
ipratropium bromide is reserved for severe exacerbations (34). The GDG was concerned that the provision 
of ipratropium bromide using an oxygen-driven nebulizer would incur additional costs to the health care 
system and/or caregivers, but considered that it could be cost-effective (moderate savings) in specific 
circumstances, probably favouring the intervention. The GDG also recognized that inappropriate use of 
ipratropium bromide in addition to poorly administered standard first-line therapy, may incur additional 
cost without much benefit.
Equity: The GDG considered that increased drug and equipment costs could contribute to inequity and 
low-resourced settings would be unfairly challenged by the required use of these interventions. The GDG 
decided that by advocating for access to ipratropium bromide through its inclusion on the EMLc, equitable 
access to the drug and its beneficial effects would be increased (12). The GDG considered that inclusion of 
a drug on the EMLc is needed to stimulate national procurement and increased demand is most likely to 
drive down local costs.
Feasibility: The GDG acknowledged that additional equipment would be necessary for implementation, 
and that masks and spacer devices are not always available, and agreed that it would only be feasible to 
implement this intervention at all levels if the equipment is procured. The GDG agreed that this 
intervention, if included on the EMLc, would be acceptable to all key stakeholders. In addition, the 
additional cost associated with using oxygen-driven nebulized ipratropium bromide would limit the 
implementation of this intervention and disadvantage resource-limited settings where oxygen is not 
available.
Implementation considerations
• Ipratropium bromide will need to be included on the EMLc, and equipment for nebulization should be 
included on the essential equipment list.
• To lower the cost of ipratropium bromide administration, use of an MDI, mask and spacer, which is as 
effective as nebulized therapy, should be considered in settings where oxygen and the equipment for 
nebulization are not immediately available.
• A 500 mL bottle spacer is an effective alternative to a conventional commercial spacer, but should be 
constructed following the methods that have been demonstrated as effective (59-61).

• In severe asthma, children should receive frequent doses of nebulized bronchodilators driven by 
oxygen, and, after improvement, treatment can be adjusted to MDI as tolerated (30).
• There is an opportunity to tailor the intervention based on the severity of the exacerbation and the 
availability of equipment.
• Once clinically stable and ready for discharge, patients and families must have a clear understanding 
of the treatment to be continued at home, how to monitor symptoms and signs, and action to take in 
case of a deterioration.
• Educating families on asthma self-management improves outcomes in children, including a reduction 
in school absence and emergency care visits (62).
• Patients should be provided with written action plans to guide home management of asthma.
• Asthma action plans based on monitoring of symptoms, rather than peak flow measurements, are 
preferred by children and are more likely to prevent acute care visits (63).
Research gaps
• An analysis of the failure rate of standard acute asthma therapy with inhaled SABA and corticosteroids.
• Investigating the effect of dose, timing, route of administration and duration of ipratropium bromide 
therapy on the effectiveness of the intervention.
• Investigating the ideal treatment options for children discharged after an acute asthma exacerbation 
who received ipratropium bromide.
• A post-implementation analysis of the effect of ipratropium bromide on referrals to tertiary centres in 
LMICs.
4.2 Second-line therapy options for paediatric asthma exacerbations
4.2.1 IV magnesium sulfate
Background
Asthma is a chronic lung disease characterized by airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness of 
airway smooth muscles. There is growing evidence that magnesium sulfate (MgSO 4) may have a role in 
managing asthma through its dual effect as an anti-inflammatory and bronchodilating agent (64, 65). 
Bronchodilatation is attributed to the blockade of calcium channels in the airway smooth muscles and 
a reduction in airway excitability. This anti-inflammatory process is due to the eradication of oxygen free 
radicles, the stabilization of T-cells and mast cells, and the facilitation of endogenous nitric oxide and 
prostaglandin release (64, 66). Additionally, magnesium sulfate acts as a beta-receptor agonist, resulting in 
a synergistic effect when administered with salbutamol (67).
Previous research and evidence reviews have shown that administering magnesium sulfate via IV or 
inhaled routes can help manage acute exacerbations of asthma. Both routes of administration are fast-
acting and effective, although the IV route has greater bioavailability but with associated with systemic 
side-effects (68). Intravenous magnesium sulfate is currently used as adjunctive therapy for severe asthma 
exacerbations. Its addition to standard asthma therapy in both children and adults has been shown to 
reduce hospitalizations and clinical asthma scores (65, 69). However, it is acknowledged that the evidence 
in the literature has provided conflicting results, with studies exploring both the IV and nebulized routes of 
administration (70-72). In the most recent review of three RCTs in 816 children aged less than 5 years with 
acute asthma exacerbation, nebulized or IV magnesium sulfate did not show any benefit in hospitalizations 
or clinical outcomes when compared to standard treatment (73).
Despite the conflicting evidence, several asthma treatment guidelines currently recommend giving 
IV magnesium sulfate to children having asthma exacerbations who have not responded well to other 
treatments, but it remains unclear whether it is safe and similarly effective for children. The evidence 
review of IV magnesium sulfate to date is inconclusive and warrants further investigation.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Recommendation 2:
IV magnesium sulfate (as a single short infusion) should be used as second-line therapy for 
severe paediatric asthma exacerbations, and for moderate exacerbations not responsive to 
standard first-line therapy with inhaled/nebulized medicines (SABA and ipratropium) and 
systemic corticosteroids in health care facilities.
Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• Current evidence does not support the use of inhaled magnesium sulfate, and IM 
magnesium sulfate has not been studied in acute asthma exacerbations.
• Intravenous infusion of magnesium sulfate relaxes smooth muscle and may result 
in hypotension, a side-effect commonly seen with the use of IM magnesium sulfate in 
pregnant women.
• It is advised that magnesium sulfate should be diluted in a compatible solution and 
administered as a single IV infusion over 20 minutes.
• The most frequent dosing regime was 50 mg/kg of magnesium sulfate diluted in 100 mL 
normal saline with a maximum dose of 2 g administered over 20–30 minutes, although it 
has been suggested that higher doses up to 100 mg/kg and prolonged infusions may be 
beneficial life-threatening asthma.
• Regular blood pressure monitoring should be included in the routine observations of 
children receiving IV magnesium sulfate.
Justification
The GDG judged severe asthma as a life-threatening condition for which early and effective treatment 
is necessary to avoid adverse outcomes and therefore made a strong recommendation in favour of IV 
magnesium sulfate, while acknowledging contextual differences in how this will be implemented. Given 
the desirable benefits, trivial non-severe adverse effects and values, acceptability, equity and feasibility, 
which all favoured the use of IV magnesium sulfate, the GDG made a recommendation in favour of IV 
magnesium sulfate as second-line therapy for severe paediatric asthma exacerbations, and for moderate 
exacerbations not responsive to standard first-line therapy with inhaled SABA and systemic corticosteroids. 
The GDG was mindful that IV access and the infusion pumps required for IV magnesium sulfate may result 
in additional costs in settings where equipment such as infusion pumps and monitoring are unavailable. 
The GDG supports a tailored approach in these settings where IV magnesium sulfate is reserved for 
children with more severe exacerbations.

Summary of evidence
This meta-analysis included nine studies of 473 children aged 18 years and younger with acute asthma 
exacerbation as defined by the study criteria and included upper-middle-income countries (Argentina, Brazil, 
Paraguay, Türkiye) (74-77) and one lower-middle-income country (India) (78). Children were recruited from 
emergency departments, and studies used various criteria for defining the severity of the exacerbations. 
In four trials, children with moderate to severe exacerbations were included based on a PEF of <60–70% 
(74, 79, 80) or a pulmonary index score >8 (81); in four trials (76-78, 82) inclusion was based on a variety 
of clinical scoring systems (83-85); and in one trial inclusion was based on clinical symptoms as per local 
guidance (75). All children received and failed to improve with standard first-line therapy, including at least 
three inhalations of SABA and systemic corticosteroids. The addition of magnesium sulfate to standard 
first-line therapy was compared to standard first-line therapy alone or in addition to placebo. Magnesium 
sulfate was typically administered as a short IV infusion diluted in normal saline and given over 20 minutes.
The critical outcomes under investigation included hospitalization, escalation of care (mechanical 
ventilation or PICU admission), length of hospital stay, morbidity (symptom improvement) and adverse 
events. When compared to placebo, the need for hospitalization was less among the magnesium sulfate 
group (RR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.54–0.90, low-certainty evidence) (79-81) and the need for non-invasive ventilation 
(RR: 0.17; 95% CI: 0.05–0.54) favoured magnesium sulfate (76). However, escalation of care to invasive 
mechanical ventilation was similar in both groups (RR: 0.35; 95% CI: 0.11–1.17, very low-certainty evidence) 
(75, 76, 82), and there was no difference in PICU admission rate (RR: 0.58; 95% CI: 0.15–2.22, very low-
certainty evidence) (82) or the length of hospital stay in hours between the two groups (MD: −78.86; 95% CI: 
−200.37 to 42.66, low-certainty evidence) (75, 76, 78, 82). One study used PEF as a proxy for improvement in 
symptoms and reported an improvement with IV magnesium sulfate (MD: 36.60; 95% CI: 33.28–39.92) (74). 
When clinical asthma severity scores were used, no difference was found (MD: −0.18; 95% CI: −1.35 to 0.98, 
low-certainty evidence) (81, 82). Additional SABA nebulizations were similar in both groups (MD: 0.14; 95% 
CI: −0.53 to 0.80, low-certainty evidence) (80, 82). The included studies did not report enough data to enable 
meta-analysis; however, minor side-effects reported included epigastric warmth (12.5%), pain (16.6%), and 
tingling and numbness (12.5%) at the site of infusion (78, 82). No serious adverse events were reported in 
any of the included studies.
Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG determined that admission to PICU and escalation to ventilation should be considered priority 
outcomes. The GDG also recognized that most children with acute asthma exacerbation who receive 
magnesium sulfate have severe symptoms and are likely to require hospitalization. There was very low-
certainty evidence that the addition of magnesium sulfate to standard first-line therapy reduced the need 
for non-invasive ventilation (RR: 0.17), ventilatory support overall (RRR: 5.8%) and decreased hospitalizations 
(RRR: 23%). Based on this evidence, the GDG judged the desirable effects as moderate.
Harms and undesirable effects
Minor adverse effects such as facial flushing, epigastric warmth, pain and tingling and numbness at the 
infusion site were reported in two studies. The GDG judged these undesirable effects to be trivial.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG agreed that most caregivers would value the avoidance 
of mechanical ventilation and PICU admission over the trivial risk of non-severe adverse effects attributed to 
magnesium sulfate administration. This view is supported by a qualitative study of parents and caregivers 
of children presenting to hospital with a severe acute exacerbation of asthma in 12 countries (high- and 
middle-income) (37). Caregivers represented in this study highlighted length of hospital stays, ICU or high 
dependence unit admission and treatment costs as the most important outcomes. There was agreement 
among the GDG that the intervention would be acceptable to key stakeholders, with the provision that 
contextual differences would be considered.
Resources required: The systematic review did not include studies providing a cost-effectiveness analysis, 
but previous studies have shown a cost benefit based on higher quality-adjusted life years and the 
avoidance of hospitalization with a number needed to treat of four when IV magnesium sulfate was used in 
acute asthma exacerbation (86, 87). The GDG concluded that using IV magnesium sulfate in acute asthma 
exacerbation may result in moderate savings to the health care system. However, due to the additional 
cost incurred for the administration equipment and staff required to administer IV magnesium sulfate as a 
slow bolus (over 20 minutes) this may preclude its use from resource-limited settings.
Equity: The GDG also decided that the increased use of magnesium sulfate for children with asthma 
exacerbation is unlikely to affect its availability for pregnant women with (pre)eclampsia as the numbers 
treated would be too small to have an impact. The GDG concluded that health equity would be increased 
by the intervention.
Feasibility: The GDG recognized that the implementation of IV magnesium sulfate would be difficult in 
resource-limited settings where infusion pumps are not routinely available. In these settings, the GDG 
suggested that IV magnesium sulfate may be reserved for the treatment of more severe cases. In addition, 
IM magnesium sulfate for the management of (pre)eclampsia in pregnancy is included in the WHO Model 
List of Essential Medicines and is widely available (88, 89).
Implementation considerations
The GDG judged the implementation of the intervention as probably feasible.
Research gaps
• Investigating higher doses and prolonged magnesium sulfate infusions in the management of acute 
asthma exacerbations.
• Investigation of IM magnesium sulfate as an alternative route of administration in children with acute 
asthma exacerbation in resource-limited settings where IV access is not attainable.

Equity: The GDG also decided that the increased use of magnesium sulfate for children with asthma 
exacerbation is unlikely to affect its availability for pregnant women with (pre)eclampsia as the numbers 
treated would be too small to have an impact. The GDG concluded that health equity would be increased 
by the intervention.
Feasibility: The GDG recognized that the implementation of IV magnesium sulfate would be difficult in 
resource-limited settings where infusion pumps are not routinely available. In these settings, the GDG 
suggested that IV magnesium sulfate may be reserved for the treatment of more severe cases. In addition, 
IM magnesium sulfate for the management of (pre)eclampsia in pregnancy is included in the WHO Model 
List of Essential Medicines and is widely available (88, 89).
Implementation considerations
The GDG judged the implementation of the intervention as probably feasible.
Research gaps
• Investigating higher doses and prolonged magnesium sulfate infusions in the management of acute 
asthma exacerbations.
• Investigation of IM magnesium sulfate as an alternative route of administration in children with acute 
asthma exacerbation in resource-limited settings where IV access is not attainable.

Recommendation 3:
IV aminophylline should not be used as second-line therapy for severe paediatric asthma 
exacerbations in health care facilities if alternative second-line options are available.
Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• The restricted use of aminophylline should be accompanied by the availability of 
appropriate inhaled SABA and systemic corticosteroids for the management of acute 
asthma exacerbation across all settings.
• In resource-restricted and rural settings, aminophylline may be the only available agent 
for the management of acute asthma exacerbations.
• If the decision is made to use aminophylline, adequate monitoring and anti-emetics 
should be used to mitigate the risk of side-effects.
4.2.2 IV aminophylline
Background
Aminophylline is a methylxanthine bronchodilator composed of theophylline and ethylenediamine. 
Theophylline relaxes the smooth muscle of the bronchial airways and pulmonary blood vessels and reduces 
airway responsiveness to histamine, methacholine, adenosine and other chemical mediators. Aminophylline 
causes non-selective modulation of intracellular calcium release, inhibition of phosphodiesterase 
and antagonism of the adenosine receptor (90). Furthermore, aminophylline stimulates endogenous 
catecholamine release resulting in inotropic and chronotropic effects on myocardium (91). Aminophylline 
has a narrow therapeutic range (10–20 mg/dL) and severe toxicity may occur at higher levels, resulting in 
tachycardia, diuresis, hypokalaemia, convulsions and sudden death due to cardiac dysrhythmia (92).
The addition of IV aminophylline to standard first-line therapy with SABA and systemic corticosteroids 
remains controversial, and treatment guidelines vary from country to country (22, 93, 94). One meta-analysis 
concluded that the addition of IV aminophylline improved lung function within 6 hours of treatment but 
reduction in symptoms, number of nebulized SABA doses or length of hospital stay, but was associated with 
significant increased risk of nausea and vomiting (95, 96). More recently, in a review of IV aminophylline use 
in adults, IV aminophylline had no beneficial effects over standard of care and resulted in a 15% increase 
in arrhythmias or palpitations (97).
Internationally, there has been a shift away from using IV aminophylline in acute asthma exacerbations 
and experts have cautioned against its continued use (22). Despite this, aminophylline is widely available, 
affordable and remains part of the limited repertoire of drugs for the management of acute asthma 
exacerbations in remote areas (98).
Based on the current available evidence and practices, there is need to define the role of IV aminophylline 
in the management of acute asthma exacerbation.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Justification
Given the trivial benefits, moderate adverse events and lower acceptability, the GDG suggested against 
the use of aminophylline in addition to first-line therapy in acute severe asthma exacerbations. This was 
driven by the low certainty of evidence that there no benefits associated with IV aminophylline, in addition 
to standard first-line therapy for acute asthma exacerbation, in the length of hospital stay, number of 
additional nebulized SABA doses needed during the study duration or improvement in asthma severity 
scores. There is moderate-to-high certainty of evidence that the IV aminophylline group had a moderate 
increase in undesirable adverse effects in the form of nausea and vomiting. The GDG recognized that 
there are settings in which aminophylline is the only available option and that there may still be a place for 
aminophylline as a second-line agent when appropriately monitored.
Summary of evidence
The evidence reviewed included nine studies of 464 children aged 18 years and younger with acute asthma 
exacerbation, as defined by the study criteria, mostly conducted in high-incomes settings, except for two 
upper-middle-income countries (Brazil, Türkiye) (99-101). Two trials (102, 103) scored severity based on the 
pulmonary index, four studies on standardized asthma severity scores (99, 104-106), two studies based on 
self-authored asthma severity score (100, 107), two studies used the Wood–Downes clinical scoring system 
(85) and the other study used a lack of clinical response to standard first-line asthma therapy (101). All 
children received and failed to improve with standard first-line therapy, including at least three inhalations 
of SABA and systemic corticosteroids. The addition of IV aminophylline to standard first-line therapy was 
compared to standard first-line therapy alone or in addition to placebo. The dosing and administration 
of aminophylline varied, but typically included a loading dose of diluted aminophylline administered as a 
short bolus over 20–30 minutes, followed by an infusion of diluted aminophylline. One study administered 
aminophylline boluses 6-hourly (101)  and three studies calculated the aminophylline infusion rate based 
on therapeutic drug monitoring (102, 103, 106). The critical outcomes included the length of hospital stay, 
morbidity (symptom improvement) and adverse effects.
When compared to placebo, the IV aminophylline group showed no significant difference in the length of 
hospital stay in hours (MD: −3.62; 95% CI: −13.05 to 5.82) (101, 103, 105, 106), number of SABA nebulizers 
needed during the study duration (MD: 0.25; 95% CI: −0.39 to 0.89) (99, 101, 103, 105, 107), asthma severity 
score (MD: 0.13; 95% CI: −0.79 to 1.06) (99, 106), percentage improvement of predicted FEV1 (MD: 7.00; 95% 
CI: −7.55 to 21.55) (103) , improvement in PEF after 1 hour (MD: −0.14; 95% CI: −0.32 to 0.04) (105)  or the 
need and duration of oxygen supplementation in hours (MD: −1.90; 95% CI: −4.37 to 0.57) (101) . Adverse 
effects observed in the IV aminophylline group included emesis (RR: 3.52; 95% CI: 2.04–6.06) (99, 102, 104, 
105, 107) and nausea (RR: 4.92; 95% CI: 2.41–10.06) (102, 104, 105). Other adverse effects such as headache 
(RR: 1.49; 95% CI: 0.52–4.25) (102, 104, 105), tremors (RR: 1.35; 95% CI: 0.88–2.06) (105, 107), abdominal pain 
(RR: 6.0; 95% CI: 0.31–115.6) (104), arrhythmia (RR: 0.40; 95% CI: 0.02–9.12) (104) , irritability (RR: 1.16; 95% 
CI: 0.70–1.95) (104) and seizures (RR: 1.01; 95% CI: 0.06–15.91) (105) were observed, but no difference was 
detected between groups.
Benefits and desirable effects
There was low-certainty evidence that the use of IV aminophylline had no significant impact on the critical 
outcome of reduction in the length of hospitalization (MD: −3.62 hours), improved asthma severity scores 
(MD: 0.13) or the number of additional doses of nebulized SABA (MD: −1.9). These findings are consistent 
with previous reviews of IV aminophylline use in children with acute asthma exacerbation, and the GDG 
judged the desirable effects to be trivial (96, 108).
