Harms and undesirable effects
An increase in both nausea (relative risk increase (RRI): 23.1%) and vomiting (RRI: 8.3%) in the groups 
receiving aminophylline were judged by the GDG as moderate undesirable effects that are best avoided in 
children with acute asthma exacerbation. The GDG considered that anti-emetics routinely administered in 
settings where aminophylline is still in use may mitigate these adverse effects. However, it was also noted 
that newer, appropriate and effective anti-emetics with fewer side-effects in children are not routinely 
available in resource-limited and remote settings where aminophylline is likely to be used (109) . Major 
side-effects such as arrhythmias and seizures were only reported in one study which found no difference 
between groups.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG determined that most providers and caregivers would 
want to avoid the adverse effects of aminophylline. This view is supported by a review of antiemetic use in 
children, indicating that nausea results in more frequent hospitalization, and would preferably be avoided 
by families (109) . The GDG agreed that a recommendation against the use of aminophylline would be 
acceptable in most settings but recognized that practitioner views on the use of IV aminophylline are often 
entrenched with personal choice and locally accepted practices determining its use (110). The GDG also 
recognized that the continued use of aminophylline due to the unavailability of alternatives will continue 
and should be addressed.
Resources required: No studies evaluated cost or cost-effectiveness, but aminophylline is known to be 
widely available and cheap.
Equity: In view of the lack of evidence supporting the use of aminophylline in acute asthma exacerbation, 
the GDG agreed that cautioning against its use and advocating for the availability of preferable drugs 
would improve access to better asthma treatment and improve equity. The ongoing use of aminophylline 
in resource-limited settings where access to alternatives is not available decreases equitable management 
of asthma exacerbations in those populations.
Feasibility: The GDG agreed that it is feasible to limit the use of aminophylline in acute asthma 
exacerbations but recognized that there may be a role for aminophylline as a second-line agent in settings 
where preferred alternatives are not available. This reality should not distract from advocating for the use 
of more efficient drugs in asthma exacerbation management.
Implementation considerations
• The restricted use of aminophylline should be accompanied by ensuring availability of inhaled SABA 
and systemic corticosteroids for the management of acute asthma exacerbation across all settings.
• It is important that a recommendation against the use of IV aminophylline should not disadvantage 
resource-restricted and rural settings where aminophylline may be the only available agent for the 
management of acute asthma exacerbations.
• If the decision is made to use aminophylline, adequate monitoring and anti-emetics should be used 
to mitigate the risk of side-effects.
• Children receiving aminophylline require clinical monitoring including heart rate, respiratory rate, 
electrocardiogram (ECG) and neurological observations.
• Where available, blood gases and serum aminophylline/theophylline concentrations should be 
considered in those already receiving oral therapy and on prolonged treatment (23).
22

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Research gaps
Important research priorities include the development of an internationally agreed core outcome set for 
future trials in acute severe asthma exacerbations and the determination of clinically important differences 
in these outcomes, which can then inform adequately powered future trials on the benefit of:
• the use of aminophylline in avoidance of PICU admission for severe paediatric asthma exacerbation; 
and
• the use of aminophylline as rescue therapy in children admitted to PICU with severe asthma 
exacerbation.
4.2.3 Subcutaneous adrenaline (epinephrine)
Background
Adrenaline is a non-selective agonist of alpha and beta adrenoceptors that causes bronchodilation through 
stimulation of beta2-adrenergic receptors leading to bronchial smooth muscle relaxation, while the alpha 
agonist effect reduces airway oedema through the stimulation of alpha receptors (111). Historically, 
subcutaneous or IM adrenaline was the mainstay of acute asthma treatment but current asthma guidelines 
do not recommend its use except in the context of concomitant anaphylaxis or angio-oedema (22, 111, 112). 
However, the administration of IM adrenaline in addition to nebulized selective beta 2 agonist for acute 
severe or life-threatening asthma remains part of many prehospital emergency guidelines and continues 
to be used by some clinicians (112, 113).
A recent systematic review and meta-analysis that evaluated the use of adrenaline administered by any 
route, compared to the administration of selective beta 2 agonist by any route in adults and children with 
acute asthma exacerbation (114). The review found limited evidence that there was no benefit from the 
use of adrenaline in addition to selective beta2 agonist in acute asthma exacerbation (114). Subcutaneous 
adrenaline did not reduce treatment failure or lead to greater bronchodilation than nebulized selective 
beta2 agonist alone.
WHO’s Pocket book of hospital care for children currently advises the use of subcutaneous adrenaline in 
severe life-threatening asthma if inhaled or nebulized salbutamol is not available (1). This practice dates 
to a time when salbutamol was not widely available. There was need to evaluate the current evidence to 
support on the use of subcutaneous adrenaline in acute asthma exacerbations.
No recommendation: 
WHO makes no recommendation on the use of subcutaneous adrenaline in the management 
of acute asthma.
Remarks
Adrenaline should be reserved for patients who present with symptoms and signs consistent 
with severe allergic reactions.
The use of IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis is described in WHO’s Pocket book of hospital care for 
children (1) and the Integrated management of adolescent and adult illness (2).
23

Justification
The GDG agreed that the evidence was too indirect to make a recommendation as standard first-line 
therapy for acute asthma exacerbation was not used in either group. The GDG agreed that inhaled/
nebulized SABA and systemic corticosteroids are the minimal standard of care for children with acute 
asthma exacerbations and should not be replaced by subcutaneous adrenaline. The use of subcutaneous 
or IM adrenaline should only be used in those who present with symptoms and signs consistent with 
severe allergic reactions.
Summary of evidence
The systematic review included one RCT comparing subcutaneous long-acting adrenaline (0.005 mg/kg) 
with nebulized SABA to nebulized SABA alone in 43 children with acute asthma exacerbation according 
to the study guidelines. Critical outcomes of interest included hospitalization, morbidity (improvement 
in symptoms) and adverse effects. No significant difference between hospitalization in the studied group 
was noted (RR: 0.38; 95% CI: 0.04–3.40) and no significant difference was found in the number of albuterol 
nebulizations needed between the two groups (MD: −0.20; 95% CI: −0.62 to 0.22). The study found no 
change between the groups in the assessment of heart rate and respiratory rate post intervention but did 
not specifically evaluate adverse effects (115).
4.2.4 IV SABA in management of acute severe asthma exacerbation
Background
The current standard of care for the management of acute asthma exacerbations includes inhaled SABA 
and systemic corticosteroids (116). SABA is a beta 2-adreneceptor agonist and binds to the beta 2 receptor, 
thereby activating adenyl cyclase which results in the conversion of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to 
cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP). This promotes bronchodilation and effective symptom control 
in acute asthma exacerbation (22). The penetration of inhaled SABA, especially into the small conducting 
airways, may be reduced due to airway inflammation associated with severe acute asthma exacerbations, 
resulting in a reduced response. It is hypothesized that IV delivery of SABA to the receptors via the systemic 
circulation may improve clinical response (117).
A previous systematic review investigated the addition of IV SABA to inhaled SABA in 104 adults and 
children and included three RCTs (118). The outcome measures reported in the trials were heterogeneous 
and only one study reported statistically significant shortening in recovery time in the IV SABA (salbutamol)

The GDG agreed that the evidence was too indirect to make a recommendation as standard first-line

Summary of evidence
The systematic review included one RCT comparing subcutaneous long-acting adrenaline (0.005 mg/kg) 
with nebulized SABA to nebulized SABA alone in 43 children with acute asthma exacerbation according 
to the study guidelines. Critical outcomes of interest included hospitalization, morbidity (improvement 
in symptoms) and adverse effects. No significant difference between hospitalization in the studied group 
was noted (RR: 0.38; 95% CI: 0.04–3.40) and no significant difference was found in the number of albuterol 
nebulizations needed between the two groups (MD: −0.20; 95% CI: −0.62 to 0.22). The study found no 
change between the groups in the assessment of heart rate and respiratory rate post intervention but did 
not specifically evaluate adverse effects (115).
4.2.4 IV SABA in management of acute severe asthma exacerbation
Background
The current standard of care for the management of acute asthma exacerbations includes inhaled SABA 
and systemic corticosteroids (116). SABA is a beta 2-adreneceptor agonist and binds to the beta 2 receptor, 
thereby activating adenyl cyclase which results in the conversion of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to 
cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP). This promotes bronchodilation and effective symptom control 
in acute asthma exacerbation (22). The penetration of inhaled SABA, especially into the small conducting 
airways, may be reduced due to airway inflammation associated with severe acute asthma exacerbations, 
resulting in a reduced response. It is hypothesized that IV delivery of SABA to the receptors via the systemic 
circulation may improve clinical response (117).
A previous systematic review investigated the addition of IV SABA to inhaled SABA in 104 adults and 
children and included three RCTs (118). The outcome measures reported in the trials were heterogeneous 
and only one study reported statistically significant shortening in recovery time in the IV SABA (salbutamol) 
group (P = 0.03) (117). The IV SABA group was discharged 9.7 hours earlier than the inhaled SABA group (P 
< 0.05) (117). In the study conducted in the PICU, there was no benefit in length of admission in the IV SABA 
(terbutaline) group (MD: −12.95 hours; 95% CI: −38.74 to 12.84) (119). A subsequent observational study in 
120 children found a 44% decrease in mechanical ventilation when IV SABA was used and the duration of 
mechanical ventilation was shorter in the group who received IV SABA prior to PICU admission (120).
Based on the limited current favourable evidence from single studies, the GDG judged the importance of 
defining the role of IV SABA in the management of acute asthma exacerbation as a priority problem.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Recommendation 4:
IV SABA should be used as a potential second-line therapy for severe paediatric asthma 
exacerbations in addition to standard first-line therapy with inhaled/nebulized medicines 
(SABA and ipratropium) and systemic corticosteroids in health care facilities.
Strong recommendation, high-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• IV SABA can be used as a potential second-line therapy, depending on the availability 
of other options. IV magnesium sulfate would be preferred as second-line therapy, if 
available (see Recommendation 5).
• IV SABA is most likely to be used in the PICU or settings where the infrastructure and 
monitoring already exist.
• Careful clinical monitoring is recommended to ensure the early identification and 
management of possible cardiovascular adverse effects, such as tachycardia, hypotension 
and arrhythmias.
• Where resources are available, it is advisable to have continuous ECG monitoring, and 
check serum electrolytes (hypokalaemia) and lactate.
Justification
Given the balance between the moderate desirable benefits, small undesirables and values, acceptability 
and feasibility, the GDG made a strong recommendation favour of the use of IV SABA in severe asthma 
exacerbations with poor response to standard first-line therapy including inhaled/nebulized SABA and 
systemic corticosteroids. Additional literature considered suggested that caregivers would value the 
moderate benefits of the intervention over the small risk of adverse effects (37). The GDG agreed that a 
strong recommendation would encourage the procurement of the IV formulations to ensure equitable 
access to IV SABA across settings.
Summary of evidence
This meta-analysis included four studies of 183 children aged 18 years and younger with acute severe 
asthma exacerbation as defined by the study criteria, mostly conducted in high-income settings except 
for one upper-middle-income country (Brazil) (75). Children were recruited from emergency departments, 
admission wards and PICUs and all children received and failed to improve with standard first-line therapy 
including at least three inhalations of SABA and systemic corticosteroids. The addition of IV SABA to 
standard first-line therapy was compared to standard first-line therapy alone or in addition to placebo. 
The dosing of SABA was varied, but typically included IV salbutamol 15–20 μg/kg over 10–20 minutes or 
terbutaline 10 mg/kg per min over 10–20 minutes followed by an infusion. The critical outcomes under 
investigation included the length of hospital stay and escalation of care (PICU admission or mechanical 
ventilation), morbidity (symptom improvement) and adverse events.

When compared to placebo, there was high-certainty evidence that duration in hospital stay was reduced 
by nearly 1 day in those who received IV SABA (MD: −23.45 hours; 95% CI: −36.09 to −10.81) (75, 117, 119, 
121). Only one study reported on the need for mechanical ventilation and found no difference among 
groups (RR: 0.13; 95% CI: 0.01–2.42) (119). The need for oxygen was reported at varying timepoints in three 
studies (75, 117, 121). There was a reduction in oxygen dependence at 2 hours in the IV SABA group (RR: 
0.27; 95% CI: 0.07–1.05), but the result was not significant (117). The duration of oxygen supplementation in 
days were less in the IV SABA group (MD: −1.73; 95% CI: −3.01 to −0.45) (75) and the need for supplemental 
oxygen at 12 hours was similar among groups, but rapid weaning occurred in those who received IV 
SABA and ipratropium bromide, rather than ipratropium bromide alone (RR: 0.26; 95% CI: 0.11–0.61) (121). 
One study showed clinical asthma severity scores improving after 2 hours in the IV SABA group), with 
a reduction in persistent moderate to severe asthma and persistent severe asthma (117) . But another 
showed no difference between clinical scores when compared between groups at 24 hours (119).
Adverse effects were reported inconsistently. No clinically significant hyperglycaemia or hypokalaemia was 
observed (117, 121). There was a higher proportion of tremor at 2 hours in the IV SABA group (P < 0.02) 
(117). In one trial, tachycardia occurred in five (29.4%) children who received IV SABA (74). In those who 
received terbutaline, six (24%) had high troponin I values, and one had an arrythmia but troponin I levels 
were not raised (121). Hypotension was documented in the IV terbutaline group (RR: 0.43), but all received 
IV fluid therapy, and none required inotropic support (121).
Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG judged the desirable effects to be moderate. There was high-certainty evidence that IV SABA 
reduced the length of hospital stay by 1 day (MD: 23.45 hours; 95% CI: 36.09–10.81). Single studies reported 
additional benefits such as a reduction in oxygen requirements (75, 121) and an improvement in clinical 
severity score in those with persistent moderate to severe asthma (P < 0.002) and persistent severe asthma 
(P = 0.02) (117).
Harms and undesirable effects
The reports on adverse effects associated with IV SABA use were heterogeneous with very low-certainty 
evidence from single studies reporting an increase in tremor (117) , troponin I levels and hypotension not 
requiring inotropes (121). Additional evidence suggested that increased troponin I levels in children treated 
with IV SABA are common, but unlikely to be associated with harm (122, 123) . The GDG therefore judged 
the undesirable effects to be small.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG agreed that providers and caregivers would probably 
value the moderate benefits of the intervention over the small risk of adverse effects. This view is supported 
by a qualitative study of parents and caregivers of children presenting to hospital with a severe acute 
exacerbation of asthma in 12 countries (high- and middle-income) (37). Caregivers represented in this 
study highlighted length of hospital stays, ICU or high dependence unit admission, and treatment costs as 
the most important outcomes. The GDG agreed that this intervention would probably be acceptable to all 
key stakeholders.
Resources required: The additional cost incurred for the administration equipment and staff required to 
administer IV SABA as a slow bolus (20–30 minutes) or infusion may preclude its use from resource-limited 
settings and the cost saving associated with decreased oxygen requirements is unlikely to balance the 
expense. No studies assessed the cost or cost-effectiveness of IV SABA, but the GDG agreed that IV SABA 
would incur at least moderate costs and that cost-effectiveness would vary depending on the setting.

Equity: The GDG also considered how the significant upfront investment required to implement IV SABA 
availability may reduce equity and unfairly challenge settings with limited resources by the required use 
of these interventions. The GDG agreed that equitable access to IV SABA would be increased through 
advocacy and inclusion on the EMLc, but the overall effect would be a reduction in equity (12). The GDG 
agreed that a recommendation favouring IV SABA may also encourage greater availability.
Feasibility: Although the use of IV SABA achieves effective bronchodilation, non-selective stimulation of beta 
adrenoceptors is associated with diverse adverse effects and the cardiovascular side-effects are of major 
concern (22). Although tachycardia, hypotension and arrhythmias were not reported in the meta-analysis, 
careful clinical monitoring is still recommended to ensure the early identification and management of the 
adverse effects should they occur. Admission to PICU or facilities with adequate monitoring is therefore 
recommended and it is likely that IV SABA will be used more frequently in settings where the infrastructure 
and monitoring already exist. Other monitoring advised: continuous ECG monitoring, serum electrolytes 
(hypokalaemia) and lactate.
Research gaps
• Investigating the costs of IV SABA administration in acute asthma exacerbations.
• Investigating the cost-effectiveness of implementing the use of IV SABA in acute asthma exacerbations.
4.2.5 Preferred second- and third-line therapy for paediatric asthma exacerbations
Background
Current guidance on appropriate second-line therapy for acute asthma exacerbation in children who do 
not respond to standard first-line therapy or those presenting with life-threatening asthma is inconsistent. 
Previous reviews have suggested IV aminophylline, salbutamol, magnesium sulfate and adrenaline as 
various treatment options, but a recent systematic review was unable to make a firm recommendation 
(95, 124, 125). The review did however suggest that IV magnesium sulfate reduces hospital admission and 
length of stay, that hospital admissions are also reduced by the addition of ipratropium bromide to inhaled 
SABA and corticosteroids, and that IV aminophylline results in more vomiting when compared to IV SABA 
(95).
International guidelines currently suggest the use of subcutaneous adrenaline in children not responding 
to inhaled SABA and systemic corticosteroids (1) or an increase in the frequency of inhaled SABA with the 
addition of inhaled ipratropium bromide when available (11). Additional options also include a dose of IV 
magnesium sulfate or a terbutaline bolus given over 5 minutes, followed by a continuous infusion (22).
Due to the lack of clear evidence to support choice of second-line therapy for acute asthma exacerbation, 
the GDG judged the importance of defining the role of each IV therapy in the management of acute asthma 
exacerbation a priority problem.

Recommendation 5: 
IV magnesium sulfate should be the preferred option for second-line therapy and IV SABA 
the preferred option for third-line therapy in severe paediatric asthma exacerbations not 
responding to standard first-line therapy.
Conditional recommendation, very low-certainty evidence.
Remarks
• A pragmatic stepwise approach to second-line therapies would be appropriate, and allow 
practitioners to choose the best possible option for their setting.
• In settings where neither preferred option is available, IV aminophylline may be considered 
as additional therapy in severe asthma exacerbations not responding to standard first-line 
therapy.
Justification
There was very low-certainty evidence in favour of magnesium sulfate to reduce hospitalization, reduce 
additional IV treatment and improve asthma severity score with no increase in undesirable effects. 
Moderate-certainty evidence is available in favour of IV SABA for its reduction of mechanical ventilation, a 
critical outcome, but at the cost of a small increase in arrythmia. However, for IV aminophylline there was 
low-certainty evidence for the trivial benefit associated with length of hospital stay, a non-critical outcome, 
and moderate-certainty evidence in increase of undesirable adverse effects in the form of nausea and 
vomiting. The GDG agreed that due to contextual differences, resource limitations and a significant cost 
difference between therapies, a pragmatic approach to second-line therapies would be appropriate and 
allow practitioners to choose the best possible option for their setting.
The GDG agreed on a marginal benefit of IV magnesium sulfate, based on very low-certainty evidence, over 
IV SABA and IV aminophylline on balance of risk and benefit. However, a stepwise approach to IV therapy 
from magnesium sulfate to SABA and then aminophylline was advised. The GDG therefore recommended 
the use of IV magnesium sulfate as the preferred option for second-line therapy over IV SABA (second 
choice) and over aminophylline (third choice) in patients with acute severe asthma exacerbations not 
responding to standard first-line therapy.
Summary of evidence
The meta-analysis investigated studies of comparative interventions to identify second-line therapeutic 
options for acute severe asthma exacerbations. The available studies were analysed in three comparative 
groups, including IV aminophylline versus other treatment, IV SABA versus other treatment and IV 
magnesium sulfate versus other treatment.

IV aminophylline versus other treatment
A total of six RCTs of 410 children aged 18 years and younger were included. Three trials were conducted 
in low-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries (Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), India) (126-
128). Children were recruited from the PICU in two studies and the emergency department, in which all 
had critical or severe asthma in three studies and moderate to severe asthma in one study (126-131) . 
All children received and failed to improve with standard acute asthma therapy, including at least three 
inhalations of SABA and systemic corticosteroids. IV aminophylline (5 mg/kg) was typically administered as 
a slow bolus over 20 minutes followed by an infusion (1 mg/kg per min) and compared to a slow bolus of 
magnesium sulfate (50 mg/kg), a slow bolus IV SABA (15 µg/kg salbutamol or 120 µg/kg terbutaline) and a 
slow bolus of IV ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) followed by an infusion (0.6 mg/kg per hour) (126-131).
A significantly higher hospitalization rate was reported in the IV aminophylline group compared to 
IV magnesium sulfate (RR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.26–1.84) (128) . There was low-certainty evidence that IV 
aminophylline decreased length of hospital stay in a pooled comparison to IV SABA and ketamine (MD: 
−12.99 hours; 95% CI: −33.13 to 7.15) (127, 130) . The rate of PICU admission was no different between

and escalation of care (PICU admission or mechanical ventilation), morbidity (symptom improvement) and 
adverse events. The length of hospital stay (MD: 12.96 hours; 95% CI: −25.16 to 51.08) and asthma severity 
scores (MD: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.36–0.96) did not differ between groups receiving IV or nebulized magnesium 
sulfate. Overall, there was very low-certainty evidence that magnesium sulfate reduced hospitalization, 
reduced additional IV treatment (RR: 7.88) and improved asthma severity score (MD: 0.97) with no increase 
in undesirable effects.
Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG agreed that the studies were underpowered to determine critical outcomes, including clinical 
improvement and the need for mechanical ventilation, for which a very large number of participants is 
required. They also agreed that using the length of hospital stay, which favoured aminophylline (MD: 
12.99 hours) as a proxy outcome for clinical improvement, is problematic, since it may be influenced by 
various aspects of health care delivery (timing of ward rounds, availability of a pharmacist) and is not solely 
dependent on the underlying disease process. The GDG judged the desirable effects of aminophylline 
over other second-line therapies to be trivial. The GDG agreed that very low-certainty evidence favoured 
magnesium sulfate for hospitalization rate (RR: 1.52), less IV treatment (RR: 7.88) and improvement in 
asthma severity scores (MD: 0.97) and agreed that the superiority of IV magnesium sulfate was consistent 
across studies. The GDG also considered the moderate-certainty evidence that IV SABA was favourable in 
preventing the need for mechanical ventilation (RRR: 4.9%), but at the cost of an increase in arrhythmia 
(RRI: 0.8%, moderate-certainty evidence).
Harms and undesirable effects
The GDG judged the undesirable effects of IV aminophylline compared to other agents as moderate, 
based on the increase in nausea (RRI: 21.9%, low-certainty evidence) and vomiting (RRI: 17.3%, moderate-
certainty evidence). The GDG also considered the moderate-certainty evidence that SABA results in a small 
increase in arrhythmia (RRI: 0.8%). Compared to IV aminophylline and SABA, magnesium sulfate, for which 
very few non-severe adverse effects have been reported, has a superior safety profile.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG agreed that a pragmatic approach to the implementation 
of second- and third-line therapies is required and that, taking contextual differences into account, these 
interventions would be valued and acceptable to all caregivers, health care providers and stakeholders 
involved.
Resources required:  Although no studies with head-to-head cost and cost-effectiveness comparisons 
were included in the meta-analysis, there will be a cost difference between different therapies, especially 
those for which additional equipment (infusion pumps) and increased monitoring is required, such as IV 
SABA. The costs would vary among different settings, and it would likely limit the use of IV SABA. The GDG 
judged the substantial costs associated with the additional equipment, monitoring and training required 
for IV SABA administration less favourable than the minimal cost and monitoring required for magnesium 
sulfate administration. Therefore, the GDG agreed that the stepwise approach would be valued, acceptable 
and equitable to all the stakeholders.
Equity: The GDG also considered that the wide availability of aminophylline may perpetuate its use as a 
second-line therapy when other options are not available.
Feasibility: The GDG agreed a marginal benefit of IV magnesium sulfate, based on very low-certainty 
evidence, over IV SABA and IV aminophylline on balance of risk and benefit and a stepwise approach to IV 
therapy from magnesium sulfate to SABA and then aminophylline is advised. In addition, IV magnesium 
sulfate is widely available for obstetric use across settings which is most likely to favour its use.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Implementation considerations
• A pragmatic stepwise approach to second-line therapies would be appropriate and allow practitioners 
to choose the best possible option for their setting.
• The burden of additional equipment and monitoring required for the IV administration of second-line 
asthma therapies, which might be a challenge and may limit its use in resource-limited settings.
• The additional cost of IV SABA is most likely to limit its use in resource-limited settings, hence the need 
for advocacy for its use in areas where the pre-existing infrastructure allows.
• Since IV aminophylline is more widely available, it may have a role as second-line therapy, in the 
absence of alternatives in the stepwise approach.
Research gaps
• Investigating the benefit of IM magnesium sulfate administration as a rescue therapy in children with 
acute severe asthma exacerbation.
• Investigating the use of inhaled magnesium sulfate as a rescue therapy in children with acute severe 
asthma exacerbations.
• Is peak flow the optimal measurement in the evaluation of moderate to severe asthma exacerbations?
4.2.6 Combination inhaler MART for the long-term management of asthma
Background
The long-term management and control of asthma symptoms, particularly in resource-limited settings, is 
largely inadequate, with approximately one in 20 children and adolescents experiencing severe asthma 
symptoms (21). Uncontrolled asthma symptoms have a significant impact on daily life, causing school 
absence, impacting negatively on education and social opportunities (7). Asthma exacerbations  
require medical review, escalation of treatment and possibly hospitalization. Without timely and effective 
treatment, severe exacerbations can lead to death.
For patients experiencing frequent symptoms requiring relief with SABA, standard practice is to introduce 
regular treatment with daily ICS (134) . Regular treatment with ICS is well established to reduce asthma-
related deaths, hospitalizations and exacerbations (135-137). According to the Global Asthma Network 
Phase I study, the proportion of children worldwide with severe symptoms taking SABA alone, without 
additional ICS, was 44.8%, with significantly higher rates in low- and lower-middle-income countries (6). In 
children using SABA monotherapy, the use of three or more canisters per year is associated with a twofold 
risk of asthma-related hospitalization or emergency department visit, with each additional canister used 
per year associated with an 8–14% increased risk of acute asthma exacerbations (138).
Adherence to daily ICS treatment is considered a challenge, and over the past decade there has been 
increasing evidence to support a new model of long-term management, using a combination inhaler 
containing both ICS (such as budesonide) and a rapid-onset long-acting beta 2 agonist (LABA) (such as 
formoterol). Rapid-onset LABA, which acts as quickly as SABA (such as salbutamol or terbutaline), can be 
used in a combination inhaler with ICS and taken as needed to relieve asthma symptoms, and also for 
regular maintenance therapy in those with more persistent symptoms (22). This has the advantage of 
simplifying an inhaler regime and ensuring that LABA therapy is not taken without ICS.
Systematic reviews assessing the use of combination inhalers as reliever or MART have included patients 
aged 12 years and older, and report favourable reductions in exacerbations and decreased exposure to 
inhaled and systemic steroids (139-141).

A systematic review of combination budesonide/formoterol MART versus current best practice (including 
inhaled steroid maintenance) conducted in 2013 reported a reduction in exacerbations requiring oral 
steroids (OR: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.70–0.98) and requiring hospitalization (OR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.45–1.44) for adults 
and adolescents (aged 12 years and older) receiving MART. Of the 224 children (aged 4–11 years) included 
in one trial, only nine on maintenance combination inhaler therapy had an exacerbation requiring medical 
intervention compared to 21 on ICS (OR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.15–0.77) (141). A later systematic review of MART in 
patients with persistent asthma did not identify any additional paediatric studies, concluding that evidence 
for children is limited. However, for those aged 12 years and older (n = 22 749, mean age 42 years), the 
data showed that the use of MART compared with ICS as maintenance therapy (with or without LABA) was 
associated with a lower risk of asthma exacerbations (140) . Subgroup analysis of those aged 12–18 years 
has not been published.
A systematic review conducted in 2021 assessed the use of combination fixed-dose beta-agonist and steroid 
inhaler as required for adults and children with mild asthma and included five studies, with two trials 
enrolling patients aged 12 years and older. Use of the combination inhaler compared to SABA (salbutamol 
or terbutaline) alone resulted in reduced exacerbations (OR: 0.45; 95% CI: 0.34–0.60), hospital admissions 
or unscheduled health care visits (OR: 0.35; 95% CI: 0.20–0.60), and an overall reduction in exposure 
to systemic corticosteroids (MD: 9.9 mg prednisolone lower). Using a combination inhaler as needed 
compared to regular ICS use appears to reduce asthma-related hospital admissions and unscheduled 
health care visits (OR: 0.63; 95% CI: 0.44–0.91) and reduce average exposure to ICS. There were no data 
included for children aged younger than 12 years (139).
The use of a combination ICS-formoterol inhaler as reliever therapy alone or MART has been recommended 
by GINA as the preferred approach in the management of chronic asthma in adults and adolescents since 
2019 (142). For children aged 6–11 years, current GINA recommendations are to consider ICS-formoterol 
MART as an alternative to medium dose ICS or low-dose ICS-LABA plus SABA reliever for those with asthma 
symptoms on most days (GINA treatment step 3) (22). A combination inhaler approach is not recommended 
by GINA for children aged ≤5 years due to insufficient data on efficacy and safety (22).
The GDG considered this evolving area of clinical practice to be a priority topic for consideration and review 
of the latest evidence.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Recommendation 6:
Combination inhaler (steroid plus fast-onset LABA) MART should be considered for children 
with persistent asthma symptoms requiring regular ICS treatment.
Conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence.
Remark:
• Although evidence was considered for children aged 4–11 years, current formulations are 
licensed for children aged ≥6 years; hence, the recommendation is restricted to children 
aged 6–11 years.
• Current evidence supports the use of combination inhaler (steroid plus fast-onset LABA) 
MART for children with persistent asthma symptoms who are already taking or planning 
to start regular ICS therapy.
• The use of a combination inhaler results in a potentially simpler regime, which may be 
more easily followed by both patients and prescribers (143).
• Children with infrequent symptoms should use SABA as needed, considering the 
concomitant intermittent use of ICS.
Justification
Evidence from a single well-designed RCT reported decreased asthma exacerbation rates overall and 
decreased asthma exacerbation rates requiring medical intervention among children aged 4–11 years 
using a combination budesonide/formoterol inhaler for MART. Safety data from this RCT and additional 
data relating to inhaled corticosteroids/long-acting beta 2 agonist (ICS/LABA) combination inhaler was 
favourable. Cost-effectiveness studies have also reported favourable outcomes for budesonide/formoterol 
MART, compared to other treatment regimes.
Although there are several publications on combination inhaler MART that included participants aged 
12 years and older, it was not possible to extract the data for those aged 12–18 years for review by the 
GDG. The GDG therefore preferred to restrict their recommendation to the age group for which data were

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Recommendation 6:
Combination inhaler (steroid plus fast-onset LABA) MART should be considered for children 
with persistent asthma symptoms requiring regular ICS treatment.
Conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence.
Remark:
• Although evidence was considered for children aged 4–11 years, current formulations are 
licensed for children aged ≥6 years; hence, the recommendation is restricted to children 
aged 6–11 years.
• Current evidence supports the use of combination inhaler (steroid plus fast-onset LABA) 
MART for children with persistent asthma symptoms who are already taking or planning 
to start regular ICS therapy.
• The use of a combination inhaler results in a potentially simpler regime, which may be 
more easily followed by both patients and prescribers (143).
• Children with infrequent symptoms should use SABA as needed, considering the 
concomitant intermittent use of ICS.
Justification
Evidence from a single well-designed RCT reported decreased asthma exacerbation rates overall and 
decreased asthma exacerbation rates requiring medical intervention among children aged 4–11 years 
using a combination budesonide/formoterol inhaler for MART. Safety data from this RCT and additional 
data relating to inhaled corticosteroids/long-acting beta 2 agonist (ICS/LABA) combination inhaler was 
favourable. Cost-effectiveness studies have also reported favourable outcomes for budesonide/formoterol 
MART, compared to other treatment regimes.
Although there are several publications on combination inhaler MART that included participants aged 
12 years and older, it was not possible to extract the data for those aged 12–18 years for review by the 
GDG. The GDG therefore preferred to restrict their recommendation to the age group for which data were 
available and for which current formulations are licensed.
The GDG agreed that the evidence probably favoured the intervention, in keeping with the findings from 
the greater body of evidence from adult literature. However, given the relative lack of evidence in children, 
the GDG chose to make a conditional, rather than strong recommendation. The GDG reflected that the likely 
uptake of a combination inhaler MART approach would depend on the relative costs of the combination 
inhaler, compared to individual SABA and ICS inhalers.

Summary of evidence
Only one study was identified which assessed the use of combination inhaler MART in children (144). The 
data were extracted, as part of a prospectively planned analysis, from a study that recruited patients aged 
4–80 years. Participants were recruited at 41 centres across five upper-middle-income and seven high-
income countries. The three-arm double-blind RCT included 341 children, aged 4–11 years, with at least a 
6-month history of asthma, and at least one clinically important exacerbation in the preceding 12 months. 
All children had been treated with ICS for at least 3 months.
A MART regimen (budesonide/formoterol 80/4.5 µg once daily maintenance plus additional inhalations 
for symptom relief) was compared to budesonide/formoterol 80/4.5 µg once daily for maintenance (fixed 
combination) or higher-dose budesonide 320 µg once daily (fixed-dose budesonide) (n = 106). Blinded as-
needed SABA medication (terbutaline 0.4 mg) was provided in both fixed-dose groups. Participants were 
followed up for 12 months.
The critical outcomes identified by the GDG reported for this study included overall exacerbation rates, 
exacerbations requiring medical intervention (hospitalization or emergency department treatment, 
treatment with oral steroids, an increase in ICS and/or additional treatment), adverse events, discontinuation 
of treatment and daily inhaled steroid dose. Changes in lung function were considered less important by 
the GDG. The methodological quality of this study was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for 
randomized trials (145) and the certainty of the evidence was determined through the GRADEpro guideline 
development tool (146).
The overall exacerbation rates were 14% (17 out of 118 patients) on the MART regimen compared to 38% 
(44 out of 117 patients) on the fixed-dose combination (RR: 0.38; 95% CI: 0.23–0.63) and 26% (28 out of 
106 patients) on fixed-dose budesonide (RR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.32–0.94). The rates of exacerbations requiring 
medical intervention were 8% (10 out of 118 patients) for patients on MART compared to 31% (36 out of 
117 patients) on the fixed-dose combination (RR: 0.28; 95% CI: 0.14–0.53) and 20% (21 out of 106 patients) 
on fixed-dose budesonide (RR: 0.43; 95% CI: 0.21–0.87).
The mean daily ICS dose was 126 µg for those using the MART regime, compared to 80 µg for the fixed-
dose combination and 320 µg for fixed-dose budesonide.
PEF measurements were higher in those receiving MART (mean morning PEF: 255 L/min) compared to 
fixed-dose budesonide (mean morning PEF: 238 L/min; P = 0.002) and fixed-dose combination (mean 
morning PEF: 242 L/min; P = 0.22). FEV1 measurements were similar in all groups.
Serious adverse events were uncommon and included asthma exacerbations, fractures and pneumonia. 
The rate of serious adverse events was lower among those receiving MART (2 out of 118 patients), compared 
to fixed-dose combination (16 out of 117 patients) (RR: 0.11; 95% CI: 0.02–0.48) and fixed-dose budesonide 
(5 out of 106 patients) (RR: 0.35; 95% CI: 0.07–1.83). Class-related effects, such as tremor, dysphonia and 
tachycardia were rare and evenly distributed between the three groups.
There was no difference in discontinuation of treatment between those receiving MART (2 out of 118 
patients) and those in the two other treatment arms (2 out of 223 patients) (RR: 1.89; 95% CI: 0.27–13.25).
Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG highlighted that the intervention under consideration was the use of a combination ICS/LABA 
inhaler to be used for both daily maintenance therapy, and for additional reliever therapy as needed. Trials 
assessing the use of a combination ICS/LABA inhaler for as-needed therapy only, in those with milder 
asthma, were not included in the review of evidence.

Recommendations for the management of asthma in children and adolescents
Overall exacerbation rates and exacerbations requiring medical intervention were reduced in participants 
receiving MART, compared to those using a fixed-dose combination inhalers or a fixed-dose budesonide 
inhaler. The use of a composite outcome “exacerbations requiring medical intervention” meant that it was 
not possible to determine the specific effect on rates of hospitalization or emergency health care use. The 
impact on lung function was minimal, with slightly higher PEF measurements recorded for the MART group 
that are unlikely to be of clinical significance, and no difference in FEV1 between the groups (147).
Certainty of evidence for all outcomes was downgraded to moderate, on the basis that the single RCT was 
sponsored by a pharmaceutical company. The GDG judged the desirable effects to be moderate.
Harms and undesirable effects
In this single RCT, the number of reported adverse events was small and favoured the use of MART. The 
daily dose of ICS was fairly comparable between those that received MART and those using the fixed-dose 
combination inhaler and much higher in those using the fixed-dose budesonide inhaler.
The GDG also considered additional safety data in children receiving ICS/LABA in a fixed-dose combination. 
Budesonide/formoterol (delivered by both metered-dose and dry-powder inhalers) was well tolerated, with 
individual mild adverse events such as dysphonia, oral candidiasis, muscle cramps, palpitations, tremors 
and tachycardia occurring in <0.2% of the overall population (148).
The GDG judged the undesirable effects to be small, based on moderate-certainty evidence, noting that 
the follow-up period of 12 months would be too short to determine long-term adverse effects.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG agreed that the critical outcomes under consideration, 
such as reduction of exacerbations, particularly those requiring medical intervention, such as hospitalization 
and emergency department treatment, would be valued by children with asthma, their families and health 
care providers. The GDG agreed that combination inhaler MART could represent an attractive alternative 
for patients, providers and health systems if it can be provided at a similar cost to conventional asthma 
treatment.
Resources required: A cost-effectiveness study in a paediatric population in China reported decreased 
outpatient service costs with budesonide/formoterol MART and comparable drug costs to alternative 
treatment regimes. MART reduced the total cost by approximately CNY 10 516 per year with a 0.12 
quality-adjusted life-year increase (149) . A cost-utility study, comparing three alternative regimes for the 
management of moderate asthma in children aged 6–11 years from Colombia, found that budesonide/
formoterol MART was more cost-effective than fixed combination budesonide/formoterol and fixed-dose 
budesonide (150). GDG members agreed that the cost and cost-effectiveness of implementing a MART 
approach would vary between different countries, depending on many factors.
The availability of combination inhalers is limited in resource-constrained settings: WHO’s 2021 NCD 
Country Capacity Survey reported that combination budesonide-formoterol inhalers were generally 
available in public health sector primary care facilities in 7% of low-income countries, 26% of lower-
middle-income countries and 42% of upper-middle-income countries (151) . However, availability could be 
facilitated if included on the EMLc. Budesonide/formoterol dry-powder inhaler (100/6 µg/dose; 200/6 µg/
dose) has been on the WHO Essential Medicine List for adults since 2017 as single-inhaler therapy for 
asthma, indicated for regular maintenance therapy, to control the disease in patients who have failed first-
line therapy, but not recommended for reliever or rescue therapy (152).

Equity: GDG members discussed concerns regarding equity due to the likely higher costs of the inhalers, 
compared to conventional SABA and ICS, and the need to familiarize and train health care workers. The GDG 
discussed that it would take time and effort to make combination inhalers widely available and affordable.
Feasibility: Feasibility would depend on ability of children to use the inhaler device effectively. In the only 
trial reviewed, the medicine was delivered using a turbuhaler, which is a type of dry-powder inhaler. The 
device is breath activated, so the dry-powder medication is automatically released when the child inhales. 
The majority of MART trials in the adult and adolescent population have been conducted using a dry-
powder inhaler. Dry-powder inhalers may be considered for use by children aged as young as 3 years. 
Metered-dose inhalers containing this combination are also available. The GDG highlighted that spacer 
devices should be available to promote the effective use of MDIs in younger children. Where commercial 
spacer devices are not available, a 500 mL bottle spacer is an effective alternative, but should be constructed 
following the methods that have been demonstrated as effective (59).
Stringent and national regulatory authority approvals for combination inhalers, including specific age 
groups and indications, will also affect the uptake of MART. In 2017, Symbicort (budesonide/formoterol 
fumarate dihydrate, NDA: 021929) was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration 
for maintenance treatment of asthma in children aged 6–12 years, having previously been approved for 
patients aged 12 years and older in 2006 (153).
Implementation considerations
• The importance of ensuring that all asthma medicines, whether for reliever or maintenance therapy, 
are delivered by an appropriate inhaler device, considering the child’s age and preference.
• Where treatment is given using an MDI, it is essential that spacer devices are available to enhance 
delivery of the medicine into the lungs.
• In the absence of commercial spacer devices, a 500 mL bottle spacer is an effective alternative but 
should be constructed following the methods that have been demonstrated as effective (59).
• For both metered-dose and dry-powder inhalers, careful explanation and regular review of inhaler 
technique are vital.
• Successful adoption of a new approach to asthma management would require comprehensive training 
of health care providers to ensure competence to prescribe appropriately and educate patients and 
their families accordingly.
• Education on inhaler use, specific to the chosen delivery device, is an essential part of asthma 
management.
Research gaps
There is a need for more data on the clinical and cost-effectiveness of ICS-LABA combination inhalers across 
the spectrum of asthma severity in children and adolescents, particularly in resource-limited settings.
Exploration of different service-delivery models for the diagnosis and management of asthma in primary 
health care in resource-limited settings.

5. Management of 
bronchiolitis in infants and 
young children

pages.raw_text:
Bronchiolitis is an acute viral infection of the lower respiratory tract that typically affects infants and 
children aged less than 2 years, and is the leading cause of hospitalization in children globally (154) . It 
is primarily caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), but other viruses including adenovirus, 
human metapneumovirus, influenza and parainfluenza contribute significantly (154, 155). Children with 
viral bronchiolitis are at increased risk of invasive bacterial infections, including pneumonia, and have a 
higher risk of developing asthma and recurrent wheezing in later childhood (156-158) . Severe disease is 
more common among preterm babies, children younger than 6 months and children with comorbidities, 
specifically, the immunocompromised and children with congenital heart disease, neuromuscular disorders 
and other chronic neurological conditions, chronic lung disease, and asthma or reactive airway disease 
(159-161). Estimates suggest that RSV disease results in more than 30 million cases of lower respiratory 
tract infection in children aged less than 5 years annually, with 3.2 million hospitalizations and 200 000 
deaths worldwide each year (162) . Acute bronchiolitis is also associated with a high economic burden 
from the utilization of health care resources, with the highest costs attributable to severe bronchiolitis in 
children with comorbidities and prematurity (163).
5.1 Clinical presentation
Acute bronchiolitis typically presents with acute onset of upper respiratory prodrome of rhinitis or 
congestion, low-grade fever and cough progressing to the symptoms of increasing respiratory distress 
(tachypnoea and increased work of breathing) and wheezing (155, 164). Common signs include tachycardia, 
tachypnoea, hyperinflated chest, hyperresonant sounds on chest percussion, wheezing and crackles. In 
children with severe disease, there may be grunting, marked retractions, cyanosis or lethargy. Apnoea is 
common in preterm babies and those aged less than 2 months. The severity of bronchiolitis can vary from 
mild symptoms to acute respiratory failure, but most cases are self-limiting and respond to symptomatic 
care at home. Complications among the hospitalized may include severe respiratory distress or failure, 
pneumothorax, myocardial injury, neutropenia, sepsis, shock and neurological complications (165, 166).
5.2 Diagnosis and management
The diagnosis and assessment of acute bronchiolitis is based on history and clinical examination. 
Laboratory investigations, chest radiographs and virological studies are not routinely indicated (13, 164) . 
The majority of children can be managed at home with supportive care on an ambulatory basis. Home 
care includes parental education about adequate feeding, nasal saline drops and the gentle suctioning 
of nostrils to relieve nasal block, and early care-seeking in case of any worsening symptoms (13, 164) . The 
current practice for those hospitalized is supportive care, including humidified oxygen therapy, adequate 
hydration and feeding, and close monitoring, with no specific interventions of proven benefit despite wide 
variability in the acute bronchiolitis care (13, 164, 167). Children with severe respiratory distress may require 
invasive mechanical ventilation, which is associated with various complications (ventilator-induced lung 
injury, infection, airway trauma, vocal cord dysfunction and need for prolonged sedation) and significant 
financial costs (168). However, various non-invasive modes of oxygen delivery are increasingly being used, 
such as HFNC, CPAP , non-invasive positive pressure ventilation and bilevel positive airway pressure, which 
may obviate the need for invasive mechanical ventilation and the complications related to it (169-173).

tachypnoea, hyperinflated chest, hyperresonant sounds on chest percussion, wheezing and crackles. In 
children with severe disease, there may be grunting, marked retractions, cyanosis or lethargy. Apnoea is 
common in preterm babies and those aged less than 2 months. The severity of bronchiolitis can vary from 
mild symptoms to acute respiratory failure, but most cases are self-limiting and respond to symptomatic 
care at home. Complications among the hospitalized may include severe respiratory distress or failure, 
pneumothorax, myocardial injury, neutropenia, sepsis, shock and neurological complications (165, 166).
5.2 Diagnosis and management
The diagnosis and assessment of acute bronchiolitis is based on history and clinical examination. 
Laboratory investigations, chest radiographs and virological studies are not routinely indicated (13, 164) . 
The majority of children can be managed at home with supportive care on an ambulatory basis. Home 
care includes parental education about adequate feeding, nasal saline drops and the gentle suctioning 
of nostrils to relieve nasal block, and early care-seeking in case of any worsening symptoms (13, 164) . The 
current practice for those hospitalized is supportive care, including humidified oxygen therapy, adequate 
hydration and feeding, and close monitoring, with no specific interventions of proven benefit despite wide 
variability in the acute bronchiolitis care (13, 164, 167). Children with severe respiratory distress may require 
invasive mechanical ventilation, which is associated with various complications (ventilator-induced lung 
injury, infection, airway trauma, vocal cord dysfunction and need for prolonged sedation) and significant 
financial costs (168). However, various non-invasive modes of oxygen delivery are increasingly being used, 
such as HFNC, CPAP , non-invasive positive pressure ventilation and bilevel positive airway pressure, which 
may obviate the need for invasive mechanical ventilation and the complications related to it (169-173).

5.3 Scope and target audience
This guideline reviews the current evidence on selected topics related to the diagnosis and management 
of bronchiolitis in children aged less than 2 years. It does not encompass all aspects of the management of 
bronchiolitis, but discusses the priority clinical aspects for primary and secondary care levels, focusing on 
controversial areas of clinical diagnosis and treatment, and addresses the following topic areas in detail:
• clinical signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of bronchiolitis;
• clinical indicators for admission;
• the role of X-ray imaging in bronchiolitis;
• oxygen therapy and delivery in the treatment of bronchiolitis; and
• the use of nebulized normal saline in the treatment of bronchiolitis.
The prioritized PICO questions discussed in section 6 are outlined in Annex 2.
The target audience for these recommendations are policy-makers and health care professionals working 
in diverse settings and with variable availability of resources, in particular those in LMICs.

6.1 Clinical signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of bronchiolitis
Guiding principle for using clinical symptoms and signs in supporting a probable 
diagnosis of bronchiolitis in an infant or child
Good practice statement 1: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting with 
cough and difficulty in breathing, a comprehensive history and assessment of clinical signs 
and symptoms should be done. A diagnosis of bronchiolitis can be suspected if they have a 
history of a prodrome of an upper respiratory tract infection with rhinitis or coryza and cough, 
followed by respiratory distress with a low-grade fever, and any presence of tachypnoea (fast 
breathing), chest indrawing and diffuse wheeze or crackles on auscultation.
Remarks
• Assessment of clinical signs should include the IMCI (3) general danger signs, 4 cyanosis, 
respiratory rate, looking for chest indrawing, listening for a wheeze or crackles, and 
measuring oxygen saturation.
• Infants with viral bronchiolitis are usually not very ill looking, and many have a prolonged 
expiratory phase of breathing associated with wheeze.
• During an RSV outbreak, a higher index of suspicion should be maintained in the differential 
diagnosis for infants presenting with respiratory symptoms.
• A comprehensive history should also elicit presence of any risk factors and comorbidities, 
such as prematurity, children who are immunocompromized, and children with asthma 
or reactive airway disease, chronic lung disease, chronic neurological conditions or 
congenital heart conditions, and breastfeeding status.
6.1.1 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified six observational studies from five countries (Australia, India, Iran (Islamic 
Republic of), Saudi Arabia and Viet Nam) with a total sample size of 1396 participants (174-179). Outcomes 
of interest were correct diagnosis, sensitivity and specificity, and the appropriate use of antibiotics. None of 
the studies looked at the diagnostic accuracy of the signs and symptoms or whether they were associated 
with the appropriate use of antibiotics. All studies were assessed as having high risk of bias owing to study 
design, some were retrospective with missing data, or had a low sample size of less than 100, or had 
reporting concerns.
4  The IMCI general danger signs are: inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, experiencing convulsions and being lethargic 
or unconscious.

Recommendations for the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young children
6.1.2 Justification
A systematic review identified only six observational studies of suspected cases of bronchiolitis, where the 
diagnosis was not confirmed. The major factors that were likely to be predictive of bronchiolitis were cough, 
nasal discharge, difficulty in breathing, fever, tachypnoea, wheeze and auscultatory sounds, which align 
with current clinical practice. However, the GDG noted that these signs were identified in cases suspected 
to have a clinical diagnosis of bronchiolitis, which is based on the very same signs and symptoms used 
for the diagnosis. In this respect, the GDG determined that, although a recommendation was not feasible 
based on the available evidence, a good practice statement could be made in line with the WHO handbook 
for guideline development (15), which would help clinicians make a diagnosis. This statement would guide 
clinicians in diagnosing bronchiolitis, since the reviewed signs and symptoms align with standard clinical 
practice and the counterfactual would not make sense.
6.1.3 Implementation considerations
Implementation will require clinicians to take into consideration the following.
• There is usually an overlap in the clinical presentation of viral bronchiolitis and bacterial pneumonia, 
and sometimes both exist or bacterial pneumonia may follow a viral upper respiratory infection.
• Differential diagnoses to be considered include viral or bacterial pneumonia, and other serious 
conditions, such as cardiac failure, gastro-oesophageal reflux, foreign body, tuberculosis, etc.
• Assessment of clinical signs should include IMCI general danger signs, 5 cyanosis, respiratory rate, 
looking for chest indrawing, listening for a wheeze or crackles, and measuring oxygen saturation.
• A child who has IMCI general danger signs, who looks very unwell, has a high fever (temperature 
>38°C) or a fever persisting for 5 days or more, or is very hypoxic should not be assumed to have viral 
bronchiolitis alone.
6.1.4 Research gaps
• There is a need for a properly powered study that looks at the diagnostic accuracy of the signs and 
symptoms of bronchiolitis.
• There is a need to determine the signs and symptoms of bronchiolitis that are associated with 
appropriate use of antibiotics.
5  The IMCI general danger signs are: inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, experiencing convulsions and being lethargic 
or unconscious.

Guiding principle for assessing infants and children with suspected bronchiolitis
Good practice statement 2: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting with 
suspected bronchiolitis, clinicians should perform a comprehensive assessment for the 
presence of risk factors and signs of severe disease.
Indications for admission include: signs of severe disease, which include IMCI general 
danger signs (inability to breastfeed or drink, vomiting everything, convulsions and lethargy 
or unconsciousness), high temperature of ≥38°C, central cyanosis or SpO2 <90%, severe 
respiratory distress, apnoea or history of apnoea, and presence of risk factors for severe 
disease, which include comorbidities,a prematurity and age <3 months.
Remarks
• The indications for admission found in the review are mostly similar to the current WHO 
guideline recommendations for the admission of severe pneumonia (1).
• Clinicians should avoid unwarranted admissions that may lead to exposure to nosocomial 
infections and avoidable hospital care costs.
• Local context should be taken into consideration, particularly the availability of follow-up 
or its accessibility, including travelling distances for patients, for example.
• The temperature threshold of ≥38°C in cases of suspected bronchiolitis is significant and 
might be justification for admission or close observation.
• Comorbidities to consider in the history include: congenital cardiac lesions, chronic lung 
disease, cerebral palsy and neurological conditions.
 
6.2.1 Justification
This guiding principle was included because an assessment of clinical signs and symptoms when 
making clinical management decisions on bronchiolitis would never not be performed. Clinicians need 
to perform a comprehensive assessment of the severity of signs and symptoms to decide which children 
with bronchiolitis need hospitalization. These signs are commonly used to assess sick children for severe 
disease, particularly respiratory involvement, and to determine when escalation of care is warranted.

6.2.2 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified eight studies that were conducted in outpatients, emergency departments 
or wards of tertiary hospitals in Asia and Europe with a total of 473 607 participants, 95% of which were 
from two very large cohort studies (180-187) . The critical outcomes measured were hospital admission, 
length of stay in hospital, ICU admission and mortality. Six of these studies had a high risk of bias, mainly 
driven by their retrospective design, missing data or misclassification or measurement biases made in 
ascertaining diagnoses of bronchiolitis retrospectively. Table 3 shows the indications for admission in 
children with bronchiolitis aged less than 2 years in these studies.

Harms and undesirable effects
The use of these signs and other measures, such as pulse oximetry, within diagnostic criteria is inconsistent, 
and they significantly overlap with signs of other conditions, such as pneumonia and sepsis. Since 
management of bronchiolitis is predominantly supportive, missing the differential diagnosis of pneumonia 
and sepsis may be harmful.
Other considerations
Admission leads to large costs of care, particularly in LMICs. In the United States of America, for children 
aged less than 2 years, bronchiolitis incurs an annual total inpatient cost of US$ 1.73 billion.
6.2.3 Research gaps
• There is a need for a well-designed study to determine the factors in the history and physical 
examination of the infant or child with suspected bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization.
6.3 Use of chest X-ray in the clinical management of bronchiolitis
Recommendation 1
In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting or hospitalized with suspected 
bronchiolitis, routine use of chest X-ray is not suggested for the initial diagnosis and 
management of bronchiolitis.
Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence.
Remarks
• Chest X-ray for hospitalized infants and children with suspected bronchiolitis should only 
be considered on a case-by-case basis; for example, in the following clinical situations:
• if there is high suspicion for other alternate diagnosis or underlying cardiac or chronic 
lung disease related to risk factors elicited on history or physical examination;
• if a child fails to respond to treatment or persistent symptoms for more than 2 weeks 
without improvement;
• if there is suspected bacterial superinfection or recurrent episodes of pneumonia;
• if there is severe respiratory distress or severe hypoxaemia requiring admission to 
high care or intensive care;
• where a complication, such as effusion or pneumothorax, may be suspected; for 
example, when there are unilateral signs of severe dullness to percussion or absent 
breath sounds.

6.3.1 Justification
Bronchiolitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination findings, including 
cough, wheezing, tachypnoea and respiratory distress. In most cases, the diagnosis can be made based on 
these clinical features alone without the need for confirmatory imaging studies. Despite the heterogeneity 
in the three studies (188-190), the outcomes were consistent that routine chest X-ray (CXR) has no clinical 
value in typical bronchiolitis, increases the risk of unnecessary antibiotic use and escalates care costs. 
Driven by these outcomes, along with the evidence that imaging is unlikely to change management 
outcomes, the GDG decided against routine CXR for suspected bronchiolitis. Routine CXR typically has a 
low diagnostic yield in children with bronchiolitis, particularly in those without signs of severe respiratory 
distress or complications.
6.3.2 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified two prospective studies and one retrospective study conducted in the 
emergency departments of tertiary hospitals in three high-income countries, with a total of 1194 children 
aged less than 2 years with clinically diagnosed bronchiolitis (188-190). All the three studies reported on the 
rates of antibiotic therapy in those that received CXR or change in management after CXR, and, in addition, 
one prospective cohort study reported on the proportion of CXRs that were inconsistent with clinically 
diagnosed bronchiolitis. The infants in the included studies had moderate to severe bronchiolitis, with a 
median age of 2.2 months. The studies had mostly low risk of bias, mainly driven study design (188-190).
The findings from the prospective cohort study suggest that 133 children with typical bronchiolitis would 
have to undergo radiography to identify one CXR that is suggestive of an alternate diagnosis (190) . In 
addition, it showed that children were five times more likely to receive antibiotic therapy post CXR compared 
to the intended management plan pre CXR. The other prospective study of 697 children evaluated the 
relationship between CXR use and antibiotic prescribing. Antibiotic use was significantly higher among 
those who received a CXR (31%, 108 out of 355) compared with those who did not (8.4%, 28 out of 342). The 
crude OR was 4.9 (95% CI: 3.1–7.8) (189). The retrospective cohort study assessed 227 children hospitalized 
for acute bronchiolitis who received a routine CXR and 35 (15.4%) children who received a second CXR 
in the event of complications. The routine CXRs showed lung abnormalities, specifically distension and/
or bronchial wall thickening (62.4%), focal opacity (19.9%) or atelectasis (17.7%). Antibiotic treatment was 
started in 29 children (12.5%) following use of first CXR (188).
Overall, the three studies suggest that CXR contributed to only partial alteration of treatment of infants 
hospitalized for acute bronchiolitis, but increased the risk of unnecessary administration of antibiotics. 
There was low-certainty evidence about the additional value of CXR in management of bronchiolitis in 
infants aged less than 2 years.
Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG determined that there was trivial benefit from doing routine CXR in all suspected bronchiolitis 
cases. There was low-certainty evidence that routine CXR was not useful in confirming the diagnosis of 
bronchiolitis, and that it contributed only partially to alteration of treatment and leads to unnecessary 
antibiotic use with no clear benefits to patients. The characteristic radiographic findings of bronchiolitis, 
such as hyperinflation and peri bronchial cuffing, are nonspecific and do not reliably differentiate 
bronchiolitis from other viral respiratory infections. Nevertheless, the GDG observed that CXR may be 
beneficial in identifying complications and the promotion of the appropriate use of antibiotics.

Harms and undesirable effects
The GDG judged the undesirable effect as small with very low certainty of evidence. The GDG observed 
that doing CXR routinely could result in increased use of unnecessary antibiotics, with the likelihood of 
antimicrobial resistance, and might delay treatment, especially in low-resource settings where X-rays are 
not easily available at lower-level facilities. Routine CXR may also lead to unnecessary exposure to ionizing 
radiation which carries potential risks, including an increased lifetime risk of cancer. In addition, routine 
CXR for children with suspected bronchiolitis can lead to unnecessary health care utilization and diversion 
of resources, overcrowding in emergency departments, increased costs and potential delays in diagnosis 
and treatment.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG determined that patients and their caregivers value 
the main outcome that is being measured and, therefore, on balance, the GDG decided on probably no 
important uncertainty or variability. However, because of the diverse settings and levels of experience 
of staff, there may be different degrees of familiarity with clinical practice guidelines. Although patients 
are likely to accept CXRs, acceptability by clinicians may vary depending on a clinician’s confidence and 
knowledge of the patient’s overall clinical condition. Administrators may not want the additional cost of 
routine X-rays.
Resources required: There was no systematic review of the resources required. However, the GDG 
observed that the direct costs will be increased, including medical consultation and specialist referrals 
for unnecessary CXR, which will increase the cost to families. In a cost analysis study of omitting CXR in 
diagnosis of acute bronchiolitis in 2009, omission of routine CXR saved Canadian dollars 59 per patient, 
primarily due to savings in X-rays and hospitalizations (191).
Equity: In low-resource settings, there may be long waiting list for CXRs and this might affect ability of 
patients to receive proper care. The GDG felt that equity is probably reduced in these settings.
Feasibility: The GDG recognized that the feasibility of routine CXR is affected by the limited financial and 
human resources in LMIC settings and the lack of capacity.
6.3.3 Implementation considerations
• Implementation will require family engagement through effective communication regarding 
the diagnosis and natural course of the illness. Caregivers should be informed that most cases of 
bronchiolitis resolve without the need for tests or medications, and that a CXR is unlikely to change the 
diagnosis and could lead to unnecessary use of antibiotics and exposure to radiation.
• Targeted quality improvement strategies that include the use of clinical champions, implementation 
of local clinical pathways based on national guidelines, focused educational delivery, educational 
materials, and audit and feedback may be required to ensure adherence (192).

6.4 Administration of supplemental oxygen through nasal bubble 
CPAP
No recommendation:
WHO makes no recommendation on the use of nasal bubble CPAP to administer oxygen rather 
than standard flow oxygen (SFO) through nasal prongs/face mask/headbox for better clinical 
outcomes.
6.4.1 Justification
The GDG observed that the available evidence was based on a single small study, in which the criteria of 
the outcomes used had varied definitions that may vary from country to country, and which did not include 
any of the critical outcomes of interest. The 1 hour of follow-up to assess the need for the escalation 
of treatment and/or change in the respiratory rate as outcomes did not provide sufficient evidence to 
make a recommendation. Pulse oximetry would have been a more objective way of measuring clinical 
improvement in hypoxia, which was not reported in this single study.
The GDG decided not to make a recommendation because of inadequate evidence and knowledge gaps 
requiring further research.
6.4.2 Summary of evidence
Benefits and desirable effects
The systematic review identified only one RCT with a sample size of 72 infants aged less than 12 months 
who were randomized to 36 in the bubble CPAP arm and 36 in the standard arm. The primary outcomes 
measured after 1 hour were change in respiratory rate, Silverman–Anderson score and Modified Paediatric 
Society of New Zealand Severity Score (193).
The findings from this study were that 14 out of 32 infants in the nasal CPAP group and five out of 35 infants 
in the standard care group had changes in respiratory rate ≥10. The mean reduction in respiratory rate was 
greater in the CPAP group (mean: 8.0; standard deviation (SD): 6.0 vs mean: 5.1; SD: 4.0; MD: 2.9: 95% CI: 
−5.3 to −0.5). Both respiratory severity scores showed greater improvement with CPAP . The Silverman–
Anderson score decreased more in the CPAP group (−0.78; SD: 0.87 vs −0.39; SD: 0.73; MD: −0.19; 95% CI: 
−0.76 to −0.12). Similarly, the Modified Pediatric Society of New Zealand Severity Score showed greater 
improvement with CPAP (−2.5; SD: 3.0 vs −1.08; SD: 1.300; MD: −1.4; 95% CI: −2.5 to −0.3). There were only 
two cases that could not tolerate the bubble CPAP (193).
Other considerations
The GDG made no comment on any other aspects of the administration of supplemental oxygen through 
nasal bubble CPAP on the evidence-to-decision framework.

6.4.3 Research gaps
• A large clinical trial with longer follow-up of patients is required comparing bubble CPAP to humidified 
high-flow nasal cannula (HHFNC) as second-line oxygen escalation therapy for infants and children 
with acute bronchiolitis where low-flow oxygen therapy is insufficient.
6.5 Humidified high-flow oxygen versus standard low-flow oxygen 
therapy
6.5.1 Background
Oxygen therapy supplementation is a commonly prescribed intervention when caring for hypoxic or 
severely ill patients. It often takes the form of standard low-flow oxygen which can deliver up to a maximum 
of 6 litres per minute or fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO 2) of approximately 0.45 via nasal cannula or 
prongs. In standard low-flow oxygen therapy, FiO 2 delivery is directly tied to flow rate, and above 6 litres 
per minute may lead to nasal mucosal irritation and drying of the passages. Humidified high-flow nasal 
cannula (HHFNC) therapy is an oxygen supply system capable of delivering up to 100% humidified and 
heated oxygen at a flow rate of up to 60 litres per minute. The high-flow system ensures delivery of a 
fixed concentration of oxygen and the generation of positive end-expiratory pressure, reduces the work of 
breathing and clears the nasopharyngeal dead space.
In clinical practice, HHFNC may be used as an alternative to CPAP systems for apnoea of prematurity and 
post extubating (194). Some of the reported advantages of HHFNC over CPAP include less trauma to the 
nares, simpler application and making it easier to care for the baby as it gives better access to the baby, 
including for skin-to-skin contact and feeding (195) . Undesired effects include nasal erosion, tiredness 
when used over long periods, bradycardia, desaturation or high carbon dioxide, and, in addition, “rain out”
