6.4.3 Research gaps
• A large clinical trial with longer follow-up of patients is required comparing bubble CPAP to humidified 
high-flow nasal cannula (HHFNC) as second-line oxygen escalation therapy for infants and children 
with acute bronchiolitis where low-flow oxygen therapy is insufficient.
6.5 Humidified high-flow oxygen versus standard low-flow oxygen 
therapy
6.5.1 Background
Oxygen therapy supplementation is a commonly prescribed intervention when caring for hypoxic or 
severely ill patients. It often takes the form of standard low-flow oxygen which can deliver up to a maximum 
of 6 litres per minute or fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO 2) of approximately 0.45 via nasal cannula or 
prongs. In standard low-flow oxygen therapy, FiO 2 delivery is directly tied to flow rate, and above 6 litres 
per minute may lead to nasal mucosal irritation and drying of the passages. Humidified high-flow nasal 
cannula (HHFNC) therapy is an oxygen supply system capable of delivering up to 100% humidified and 
heated oxygen at a flow rate of up to 60 litres per minute. The high-flow system ensures delivery of a 
fixed concentration of oxygen and the generation of positive end-expiratory pressure, reduces the work of 
breathing and clears the nasopharyngeal dead space.
In clinical practice, HHFNC may be used as an alternative to CPAP systems for apnoea of prematurity and 
post extubating (194). Some of the reported advantages of HHFNC over CPAP include less trauma to the 
nares, simpler application and making it easier to care for the baby as it gives better access to the baby, 
including for skin-to-skin contact and feeding (195) . Undesired effects include nasal erosion, tiredness 
when used over long periods, bradycardia, desaturation or high carbon dioxide, and, in addition, “rain out” 
in the circuit can result in lavage and apnoea (196, 197). Studies have shown HHFNC to be safe as an initial 
respiratory management, and it is thought to be of benefit for children with bronchiolitis compared with 
standard oxygen therapy or nasal CPAP (198).

6.5.2 Justification
The recommendation in favour of HHFNC was driven by the moderate certainty of evidence of benefit for 
the resolution of symptoms/signs such as respiratory rate, heart rate and oxygen saturation, which the 
GDG considered to be critical outcomes. The GDG also considered the reduction of 0.85 of a day of length 
of stay in ICU as a clinically important outcome in a situation of a peak RSV epidemic, when there are often 
too many infants that need hospitalization, as this may save the lives of those who are waiting for hospital 
beds. Consequently, the GDG issued a conditional recommendation for high-flow oxygen rather than SFO. 
However, the GDG also noted that if the patients started on SFO have responded well, they do not need to 
be changed to HHFNC.
6.5.3 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified seven RCTs comparing HHFNC and SFO conducted in six countries in 
Africa, Asia and Europe, with a total of 2197 infants and children with moderate to severe bronchiolitis 
(198-204). The HHFNC studies titrated the fraction of inspired oxygen used to maintain oxygen saturation 
in a pre-specified range, and the SFO used a variety of delivery methods including nasal prongs, face masks 
and headbox oxygen. All seven studies reported on length of hospital stay and resolution of symptoms, 
five studies on escalation to the ICU (199, 201-204), and only three studies reported on adverse events 
(201-203). Although all were RCTs, all studies had some bias driven by lack of masking/blinding to the 
intervention, and some had crossovers from the SFO to the HHFNC arms due to treatment failure.
The mean length of stay in hospital was lower in infants that received HHFNC compared to SFO (weighted 
mean difference (WMD): −0.40 days; 95% CI: −1.071 to 0.27; low-certainty evidence), but this finding was 
not statistically significant. Two studies reported on length of stay in the ICU; the mean length of stay in 
the ICU was lower among infants who received HHFNC compared to the standard of care, which was SFO 
(WMD: −0.85 days; 95% CI: −2.39 to 0.69); however, this finding was not statistically significant (200, 202). In 
five studies, similar findings that there were fewer infants escalated to the ICU in the HHFNC arm than in 
the SFO arm (risk ratio (RR): 0.94; 95% CI: −0.57 to −1.53, moderate-certainty evidence), although again this 
was not statistically significant (199, 201, 203, 204) . HHFNC was associated with higher rates of symptom 
resolution compared to standard oxygen therapy (RR: 1.15; 95% CI: 1.08–1.21; four RCTs including 1887 
participants). This equates to 117 more children per 1000 achieving treatment success (moderate-certainty 
evidence) (199-202).
Seven types of adverse events were reported that were experienced by a total of 19 infants, including 
apnoea (two infants on HHFNC, three on SFO), epistaxis (two infants on SFO), inhaled condensation (one 
infant on HHFNC), oxygen desaturation (one infant on HHFNC), oxygen tube disconnection (two infants on 
SFO), pneumothorax (one infant on HHFNC, one infant on SFO) and transient bradycardia (three infants 
on HHFNC, two infants on SFO) (201-203). When “any adverse event” in the two trial arms were compared, 
infants that received the HHFNC intervention experienced 57.9% (11 out of 19 infants) adverse events 
compared to 42.1% (8 out of 19 infants) among those who were administered SFO (201-203).
Overall, there was moderate certainty of evidence of higher treatment success among those receiving 
HHFNC therapy, and moderate certainty of evidence of the length of stay in ICU and escalation to ICU for 
further respiratory support, but low certainty of evidence the same length of stay in hospital. There is no 
evidence to suggest HHFNC brings about substantially more adverse events than SFO.

Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG determined that anticipated desirable effects were moderate, driven by the moderate certainty 
of evidence of higher treatment success among those receiving HFNC therapy compared to standard low-
flow oxygen therapy. There was little impact on the duration of hospital stay, or on the length of stay in ICU 
and escalation of treatment.
Harms and undesirable effects
The GDG determined that the undesirable effects were small given that there was no serious adverse 
events recorded when compared to standard low-flow oxygen therapy. Adverse events reported included 
apnoea, epistaxis, inhaled condensation, oxygen desaturation, oxygen tube disconnection, pneumothorax 
and transient bradycardia. There were no differences between HHFNC and SFO therapy in terms of the 
incidence of adverse events: 57.9% in the HHFNC group compared to 42.1% in the SFO group.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG observed that patients and their caregivers will value the 
main outcomes that are being measured, and, therefore, decided on probably no important uncertainty 
or variability. Stakeholders, including caregivers and clinicians, are more likely to look at the outcome as 
acceptable.
Resources required: There was no systematic analysis on the resources required. However, the GDG 
considered the possible direct costs as more oxygen therapy is required with HHFNC, along with medical 
devices and overhead costs. However, in one study, HHFNC was found to be cost-effective compared to 
oxygen by nasal cannula in an infant with bronchiolitis (206).
Equity: The GDG determined that the recommendation will probably increase equity if it is rolled out as a 
programme.
Feasibility: Additional considerations that the GDG recognized as influencing feasibility include limited 
financial and human resources in some settings that may hinder the implementation of the intervention. 
The evidence from contexts and settings where the intervention has been widely deployed suggests that 
a comprehensive implementation process and a robust therapy protocol need to be integral to initiating 
and managing HHFNC in all hospital locations, including appropriate patient selection and staff education 
(207). This intervention requires increased resource requirements, financial requirements, and retraining 
health care workers. These factors may limit the feasibility of implementation in some LMIC settings.
6.5.4 Implementation considerations
• Ensuring high-quality care and patient safety.
• Regular assessment and monitoring of patient vitals (breathing frequency, heart rate, SpO 2), 
device settings (FiO2, flow), respiratory pattern, breath sounds and comfort level with the device 
are prerequisites for high-quality care and improved patient safety (207).
• A written protocol specifying the clinical indications and contraindications to guide the initiation 
and management of patients while on HHFNC therapy should be in place.
• Staff should be trained on the HHFNC protocol, the device, appropriate flow rates according to 
weight and age, and on regular monitoring of patients.

• Health system considerations.

• Health systems in LMICs are overburdened so there is a need to develop health staff with the

6.6 Nebulized hypertonic (3%) saline versus no hypertonic saline
6.6.1 Background
Bronchiolitis is caused by a viral infection and often leads to hospitalization due to respiratory distress. 
Bronchiolitis occurs because of the inflammation of the lining of the epithelial cells of the small airways in 
the lungs causing mucus production, inflammation and cellular necrosis of these cells. It is the inflammation 
of these cells that can obstruct the airway and, ultimately, result in wheezing. Treatment primarily focuses 
on supportive care, as there are limited effective pharmacological therapies.
Hypertonic saline (a strong or highly concentrated, usually ≥3%, sterile saltwater solution) breathed in as 
a fine mist using a nebulizer may help relieve wheezing and breathing difficulty (208). It is thought to work 
by reducing airway oedema through osmotic effects, enhancing mucociliary clearance and rehydrating 
airway surfaces (209). However, studies do not consistently provide evidence for a clear long-term benefit 
of using nebulized hypertonic saline.
Recommendation 3:
In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting or hospitalized with bronchiolitis, a 
trial of nebulized hypertonic saline (3%) is suggested rather than no nebulization.
Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence.
Remarks
• The majority of studies used a comparison with normal saline which may underestimate 
the effect of hypertonic saline.
• A trial of nebulized hypertonic saline in an individual patient may aid in clearance of 
secretions, but might not always be effective.
• Health facilities experience overcrowding during peak RSV season, making any reduction 
in the length of hospital stays through the use of nebulized hypertonic saline especially 
valuable.
• Health care workers should be aware that hypertonic saline can induce bronchoconstriction 
and may often require co-administration with bronchodilators.

6.6.2 Justification
The recommendation for nebulized hypertonic saline was mainly driven by a modest reduction in the length 
of stay among infants hospitalized with acute bronchiolitis, reduction in the risk of hospitalization among 
outpatients and emergency department patients, and the earlier resolution of symptoms. A reduction of 
hospital stay for even less than 1 day was considered clinically significant, particularly in RSV epidemic 
situations, although the certainty of the evidence was low to very low for all outcomes, mainly due to 
inconsistency and risk of bias. In addition, nebulized hypertonic saline seems to be cost-effective and a 
safe treatment in infants with bronchiolitis, with only minor and spontaneously resolved adverse events.
6.6.3 Summary of evidence
A systematic review identified 38 RCTs conducted over 20 years in Africa, the Americas, Asia and Europe, 
involving a total of 5114 infants and children with bronchiolitis (208) . Study sample sizes ranged from 
40 to 772, and patients were followed up for 60 minutes to 72 hours for primary outcomes. All the trials 
used nebulized hypertonic saline alone, or in conjunction with bronchodilators as an active intervention, 
and nebulized normal (0.9%) saline or standard treatment as a comparator in children under 24 months 
with acute bronchiolitis. The primary outcome was length of hospital stay for inpatient trials or rate of 
hospitalization for the outpatient or emergency department trials. Other study outcomes included were 
duration of oxygen therapy, resolution of symptoms and adverse events (208).
Hospitalized infants treated with nebulized hypertonic saline may have a shorter mean length of hospital 
stay compared to those treated with nebulized normal (0.9%) saline or standard care (MD: −0.46 days; 95% 
CI: −0.56 to −0.36, low-certainty evidence). The risk of hospitalization was reduced by 90 per 1000 patients 
for nebulized hypertonic saline compared with nebulized normal saline plus salbutamol and was reduced 
by 112 when compared to normal saline alone. Infants and children who received hypertonic saline had a 
lower number of days to resolution of wheezing (lower by 1.16 days), cough (lower by 0.92 days), pulmonary 
crackles (lower by 1.42 days) compared to those who received normal saline (low-certainty evidence). The 
13 trials included in the review (2792 infants; 1479 treated with hypertonic saline, of which 416 (28%) were 
co-administered with bronchodilators and 1063 (72%) treated with hypertonic saline alone) reported at 
least one adverse event, such as worsening cough, agitation, bronchospasm, bradycardia, desaturation, 
vomiting and diarrhoea, most of which were mild and resolved spontaneously (low-certainty evidence) 
(208).
Overall, nebulized hypertonic saline may modestly reduce the length of stay among infants hospitalized 
with acute bronchiolitis and may slightly reduce time to the resolution of symptoms. Treatment with 
nebulized hypertonic saline may also reduce the risk of hospitalization among outpatients and emergency 
department patients. Nebulized hypertonic saline seems to be a safe treatment in infants with bronchiolitis, 
with only minor and spontaneously resolved adverse events. The certainty of the evidence was low to very 
low for all outcomes, mainly due to inconsistency and risk of bias.
Benefits and desirable effects
The GDG judged the desirable effects of nebulized hypertonic (>3%) saline over 0.9% saline as moderate, 
driven by a clinically significant reduction in length of hospital stay, and reduced hospitalization and 
readmission rates. The GDG noted that that in peak RSV epidemic season, a reduction of hospital stay for 
even less than 1 day should be considered significant, depending on the setting. In addition, nebulized 
hypertonic saline contributed to earlier resolution of wheezing, cough and pulmonary crackles when 
compared to the other interventions. The duration of oxygen therapy was also reduced by 15 minutes in 
the hypertonic saline group, although this was not statistically significant.

hypertonic saline contributed to earlier resolution of wheezing, cough and pulmonary crackles when 
compared to the other interventions. The duration of oxygen therapy was also reduced by 15 minutes in 
the hypertonic saline group, although this was not statistically significant.

Harms and undesirable effects
The GDG judged the undesirable effects as trivial, and although there were more adverse effects in the 
hypertonic saline treatment arm (4.6%; 67 out of 1449 patients) than standard care (2.3%; 30 out of 1291 
patients), this difference was not statistically significant. Nebulized hypertonic saline seems to be a safe 
treatment in infants with bronchiolitis, with only minor and spontaneously resolved adverse events. In 
addition, the GDG noted that the use of hypertonic saline might lead to 13 more adverse events per 1000 
children, although the confidence interval ranged from eight fewer children to 64 more children.
Other considerations
Preferences, values and acceptability: There might be variability in how caregivers will value this main 
outcome. Nebulization involves placing a mask on the child’s face and this might raise anxiety levels in 
some parents; however, most stakeholders will probably accept the intervention.
Resource required: By reducing hospital stay and admission rate, the use of hypertonic saline may be 
cost saving and, therefore, the GDG decided that the resources required were negligible. In one study, 
the nebulized 3% hypertonic solution was cost-effective in the inpatient treatment of an infant with 
bronchiolitis (210).
Equity: Equity is most likely to vary depending on the context, such as the availability of nebulizers/masks, 
infrastructure, etc., and patients in rural settings might be disadvantaged. Hypertonic saline may not be 
available, even though it is not costly. The supply chain issues for nebulizers/masks and the quality of 
nebulizers during epidemics, as well as the education of parents, will affect implementation.
Feasibility: The considerations looked at when assessing the feasibility of implementation included stock-
outs of nebulizers and the quality of nebulizers, but the GDG was of the opinion that implementation was 
probably feasible.
6.6.4 Implementation considerations
• Caregivers need to be educated and counselled on the value of nebulization.
• When recommending the use of hypertonic saline nebulization on a large scale, especially during 
bronchiolitis epidemics, availability and stocks need to be addressed.
• The rules for discharge from hospital vary by hospital and by country, and even by age of the admitted 
infant, meaning that hospital stays for a 3-month-old may be different from those of a 15-month-old.

6.6.5 Research gaps
• Future studies should examine older populations, including children aged between 12 months and 
24 months, implement post-randomization limitation of bias (masking), and report the adverse events 
experienced by participant level.
• Other research questions include:
• what is the number of doses required for resolution of symptoms and signs?
• what is the optimal dosing regimen for nebulized therapy in bronchiolitis?
• what is the age distribution of bronchiolitis cases?
• what is the length of stay for children aged less than 6 months who are nebulized?
• what is the effect of nebulized therapy on feeding tolerance and oral intake in infants with 
bronchiolitis?
• what clinical signs or diagnostic approaches are best in differentiating bronchiolitis from asthma?

pages.raw_text:
Monitoring and evaluation will be built into the dissemination and implementation process to provide 
data and information on uptake, implementation and impact of this guideline. In collaboration with the 
monitoring and evaluation team of the Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent 
Health and Ageing, WHO, the data on country- and regional-level adoption of the recommendations will 
be monitored and evaluated in the short-to-medium term in Member States, through the WHO sexual, 
reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health policy survey (211). This survey is conducted 
every 4 years.

8. Dissemination, 
adaptation, implementation 
and update of the guideline

pages.raw_text:
As this is a global guideline, Member States are expected to adapt the recommendations to their setting, 
considering feasibility, resource availability and other considerations at the national and subnational 
level. WHO regional and country offices can assist with the adaptation processes. The dissemination and 
implementation of this guideline is to be considered by all stakeholders involved in the provision of care 
for children and adolescents.
8.1 Derivative products
These recommendations are part of the consolidated evidence for the updates of the Pocket book of hospital 
care for children (1) and the Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) chart booklet (3), which are 
the main derivatives of these recommendations. In addition to these publications, digital adaptation kits, 
training manuals, assessment tools and job aids will be updated to provide consistent implementation 
guidance.
8.2 Dissemination
An executive summary containing the recommendations, remarks, implementation considerations and 
research priorities will be prepared for public dissemination. WHO will also develop derivative tools to aid 
understanding and adaptation of these recommendations to local contexts.
The recommendations and derivative tools will be disseminated through the WHO website, and targeted 
webinars, through a broad network of international partners, including WHO regional and country offices, 
ministries of health, professional organizations, universities, WHO collaborating centres, other United 
Nations agencies and nongovernmental organizations, among others. Updated recommendations are 
also routinely disseminated during meetings and scientific conferences attended by WHO representatives.
The executive summary and recommendations from this publication will be translated into the official 
United Nations languages for dissemination through the WHO regional and country offices and during 
meetings organized by, or attended by, staff of the Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child 
and Adolescent Health and Ageing and the Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental 
Health, WHO. Technical assistance will be provided to any WHO regional office wanting to translate these 
recommendations into any of their languages. In addition, the publication of journal articles presenting the 
recommendations and key implementation considerations will be considered in compliance with WHO’s 
open access and copyright policies.
To ensure that these recommendations have a positive impact on asthma in children and adolescents and 
on bronchiolitis in infants and young children, coordinated action between WHO, other agencies, national 
departments of health and other key stakeholders is needed. National and subnational working groups 
should assess current national guidelines and protocols and determine whether development of new 
guidelines or updating of existing guidelines is required in line with these new WHO recommendations. 
WHO staff at the headquarters, regional and country levels, as well as international agency partners 
and international professional societies and national professional associations, can support national 
stakeholders in developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols, and optimizing their 
implementation.
In the context of humanitarian emergencies, the adaptation of the current recommendations should 
consider their integration and alignment with other response strategies. Context-specific tools and toolkits 
may be required in addition to standard tools to support the implementation of the recommendation in 
humanitarian emergencies.

8.3 Adaptation
Public child health programmes require supportive policies and health care services that enable the proper 
access to quality services and medicines. WHO headquarters will work with WHO regional and country 
offices to assist with the introduction, orientation and adaptation processes. For most Member States, an 
intensive and resource-heavy adaptation process will not be necessary. All efforts were made to ensure 
that, where possible, the recommendations align with accepted clinical decision-making algorithms. 
However, even if the adaptation process is not intensive, ministries of health will have to update their 
national standard treatment guidelines based on the Pocket book of hospital care for children (1) and the 
Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) chart booklet (3), update their training curricula and also 
develop plans for building capacity for health care workers on the updated clinical algorithms.
8.4 Implementation
There are a number of important implementation considerations that have been highlighted in the 
guideline for end-users as they implement these recommendations. These are necessary in order to provide 
accessible, high-quality health services for the management of asthma in children and adolescents, and 
the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young children. These considerations may assist policy-
makers, clinicians and other stakeholders to better prepare for implementation. Member States and other 
end-users need to ensure that the necessary policies, regulations, infrastructure, supplies and skilled and 
competent personnel are in place.
Local professional societies and training institutions have an important role in implementation, and an 
all-inclusive and participatory process should be encouraged. National health systems must ensure that 
supplies of medicines and commodities such as suitable monitoring are available in health care facilities 
where services are provided. In settings where a new practice is introduced (or where recommended 
practices are changed), additional training and monitoring may be required. In contexts with high rates of 
personnel turnover, pre-service training and regular opportunities for ongoing training and competency 
assessment are particularly important.
8.4 Updating
The WHO Secretariat for these recommendations will continue to follow developments in the research 
on the prevention, diagnosis and management of asthma and bronchiolitis, particularly for questions 
for which the certainty of evidence was found to be low or very low. If new evidence emerges, or other 
important considerations arise that may impact the current recommendations, the Department of Sexual, 
Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing, WHO, will coordinate an update of this 
guideline, following the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development (15).
Unless new evidence necessitates an earlier review, at 5 years from publication of this guideline, the 
Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing, together with 
its internal partners, will conduct systematic reviews of the relevant evidence and appraise the need 
for updating or revalidating the current guideline. WHO will seek stakeholder input on the scope of the 
updated guideline, as new interventions and considerations emerge.

Annex 1. Management of 
conflicts of interest for the 
Guideline Development Group
In accordance with WHO policies and procedures for guideline development, all members of the Guideline 
Development Group (GDG) were required to declare any potential conflicts of interest prior to their 
involvement. This was done through the completion and electronic submission of the standard WHO 
Declaration of Interests (DOI) form.
In addition, all GDG members, methodologists and external reviewers signed confidentiality agreements 
to ensure the integrity and impartiality of the guideline development process.
All submitted DOI forms were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat. Any declared interests were assessed 
and managed in line with the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development 6 and 
WHO’s Declarations of interests for WHO experts. 7 Where a declared interest was considered potentially 
significant, appropriate measures were taken. These included conditional participation, partial exclusion 
from specific discussions or full exclusion from the guideline process, depending on the nature and extent 
of the interest.
At the beginning of each GDG meeting, participants were asked to declare any new or updated interests. 
In cases where a GDG member had contributed to a study that informed the evidence for a specific 
recommendation, that member was recused from the relevant discussions and decision-making, as 
documented in the meeting records.

• Combination of signs and symptoms • Current practice

• Sensitivity and specificity
• Appropriate use of antibiotics

bronchiolitis, what are the clinical indicators for admission?
Population
Children aged less than 2 years with suspected bronchiolitis

• Combination of severe signs and symptoms

respiratory distress, severe chest indrawing, 
hypoxaemia (SpO2 <90%))
• Current practice
Outcomes
• Priority outcomes: hospital admission
• Prolonged stay in hospital
• Intensive care unit admission
• Mortality
